utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I apologise for the delay. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. Good morning to everybody. Good morning, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, we spoke about the incident involving children. Let me just ask you briefly. The bus that we are talking about and that we saw passing through the check-point, was it the same bus which carried the children or was the footage simply taken in order to make an impression, a full impression of the event? We can check that by checking the registration plates. The police records must reflect the registration plates of the bus. Did your cameraman tell you whether that was, indeed, one-and-the-same bus or was it just any random bus whose photo he took just to make an impression?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could tell from -- what we call in the TV businesses the rushes, which is the raw tape -- we had the original tape on which the pictures are recorded, and you can tell from that rushes tape if it was all shot at the same time, contemporaneously, from the time code on it, the electronic time code. So I have no doubts about the veracity of the pictures, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be possible to establish what footages were made in your presence, as opposed to those that were made in your absence, that were made by either your cameraman, in your absence, or by some other agency, and what is the proportion between one's and the others'? How many of those footages did you actually witness while they were being made, while they were being recorded?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the story about the children on the bus and the funeral or in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In general, yes, in general.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say -- I mean, the way that the television news business works is that we have alliances with other broadcasters and we share material, so it's common to use material from different sources in the course of one report. In Sarajevo, that was also the case, because there was a pool, in other words, an arrangement to share pictures, between the main television news agencies to which we subscribed. And we had that arrangement for safety reasons, the argument being, Why have two cameramen shooting in a dangerous place while you -- putting their lives both at risk when you could have one? However, because it was a small area, during the war in Sarajevo, I would say I was present very often for 100 per cent of the material that was being shot, even if the pictures that we had -- that we were using weren't from our camera, if there was, on occasion, more than one camera there. And on occasions, no, I wasn't present, but we're careful about the provenance of our video, so we would check where it came from. And if, on occasion, for example, like the -- you may recall from one of the exhibits, one of the videos, there were some pictures of Serbs who were shot by snipers coming from the Bosnian Government side. Now, that was -- those were pictures that reached us indirectly. In fact, I think they probably reached London and they were described to us over the phone. So I couldn't have been there when that was shot. But we were given details, and the people in London were satisfied that those pictures of the Serbs being shot were what they said they -- what they purported to be, so we put them into the piece. However, I'd say that the providence of the material is a big issue for the television news business, and we work very hard to make sure that the pictures that we -- that we use are honest and decent and truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. I apologise. And now this is what I want to know: We have the visual. How does one come up with the textual part of the news if the visual is received from others? How do you form the news, and how reliable the news is, in the criminal sense? Is it reliable, in the criminal and legal sense?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I hope it's reliable in every sense, and we try very hard for it to be accurate. On occasion, mistakes are made. You know, you're working under heavy pressure of time, heavy dead-lines, and -- but we do try. We try very hard. You know, we're not slap-dash, particularly when it's a very important story, as all the stories in the former Yugoslavia were, because they concerned life and death. So I would say that it is reliable. And you asked how the textual part of the news is put together. Well, I would write it, and I would receive information through various sources, some of which we were discussing yesterday, and put it together in a way that works with the pictures. And the thing about television news is that it's not like writing a newspaper article. You have to write -- you have to use words that complement the vision that you see and the sound that you hear and take it all together. So, for example, a newspaper reporter would describe -- maybe describe everything that happened, but I don't have to use words to describe things if you can see them. So I have to choose words that add something extra, which is lucky. It's important to do that, because we have very -- the numbers of words we write are very, very small. You know, you write -- it's three words a second, and so, say, in a two-minute news report, there isn't many words, whereas a newspaper reporter might write 800. So I might write 250, 300, something like that, no more than that; 350 maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this extensive overview of your job. Now I'm going to try and ask you as many questions as possible that you will be able to answer by just yes or no. I believe that you said that the Serbs did not need to know about the funeral, that there was actually a funeral going on. Does that mean that you do not necessarily think that the Serbs always had an intent or they had an intent to shoot at the people at the funeral, because there were people there whom they did not necessarily have to have a visual contact with?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't answer that with a single word. No, I think the point I was making was that it wasn't a show put on by the Bosnian Government side, in my opinion, for the television cameras, because the point I made was that shells landed frequently when television cameras weren't there. So my question would be -- sorry, my answer would be why -- my rhetorical question would be: Why put on a show like that and shell the graveyard for the TV cameras at a time when TV cameras weren't there? Because the point I was making was that on their side of the lines, they would know when the funeral was going on or know another event was going on there, so they could -- you know, if they wanted to, they could -- if they were doing something like that, then they would be able to see that we were there. But shelling of that graveyard happened sometimes when TV cameras were there, sometimes when TV cameras weren't there, and quite often when they weren't there. You could see that by the damage to the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you don't know that, Mr. Bowen. Neither do I. We don't know that. However, let me ask you this: The footage that the Prosecution showed as P01993 [as interpreted] has been shown here and admitted to illustrate a claim, and the claim was that the Serbs would fire a shell and then they would wait for a couple of minutes for people to turn up, and then fire a second shell. Did the children get killed from a shell that hit the bus, or the second shell, or how did they get killed? Which shell killed the children?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The children on the bus, you're referring to? They were shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to get the numbers straight, that was not P1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The correct number is ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't know, because I don't know what Dr. Karadzic is referring to. But P1993 is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it is -- that P1993 was allegedly part of P2078, we're told. Does it satisfy you, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm actually a little bit -- are we talking about 1993 or 1933, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right, I understood. And the transcript reads "1993," and that's why I arose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed. Sorry for the interruption, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, are we referring to the piece which was about the bus, the attack on the bus, itself? Is that that particular piece of evidence, that particular video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we not talking about shelling --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We're talking about the funeral or the bus? I'm not clear which one we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the funeral. The material from the funeral was used to prove that the Serbs would fire the first shell first, then wait a couple of minutes, then wait for the rescuers to gather, and then fired a second shell in order to increase the number of casualties. Was that the case in this particular instance?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say I did not make that point. I didn't make that point in the script and I didn't make that point in court yesterday. That's a point, sir, that I think you're making. I didn't make that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you this: You said that you'd heard rumours that the Muslim side was also in the process of shooting at their own people in order to inspire sympathy among the representatives of the international community and that you heard that from General MacKenzie; right? Could you please -- or, rather, an associate of General MacKenzie. Could you tell us the name of that person, General MacKenzie's associate, who told you that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you that because I'm not going to reveal my source, and, besides, I don't have the name, anyway, at the forefront of my mind, at the tips of my fingers. And I only heard that information, I have to stress, towards the end of that particular trip to Sarajevo, which was my first one to the -- to the war. So, therefore, after the funeral incident and so on. It was just as I -- more or less as I was leaving, this -- one of General MacKenzie's staff spoke to me and said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You write about that in paragraph 39 of your consolidated statement, and you express doubt. You said: "I didn't see any proof to that effect." And that's why you do not believe that story. I would like to show you two documents, very briefly, to show you that those were not just rumours, but very serious doubts harboured by the United Nations representatives.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce D681. Can that be produced in e-court, please, D681.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you agree that this is a report that was sent to General Rose from the Sarajevo Sector on the 26th and 27th October 1994, I would like to move on to the following page, please. And here there is a description of an incident which happened around Bratstvo and Jedinstvo Bridge, where eight people were injured. Can you please look at the last bullet, where it says: [In English] "and corps operations by Bosnian officials indicate shots came from Bosnian-held territory (see map ..." And so on and so on. [Interpretation] Does this sound convincing, Mr. Bowen, or do you also have doubts about this report?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't possibly have an opinion about this report, because I wasn't there, I didn't report on the story, it's the first time I've seen the document, and, you know, I can read the report as well as you can and what it says, and it clearly seems to be a genuine document, but I wasn't there. I mean, the one point that occurs to me as a journalist, looking at this for the first time, is that if the Bosnian side was up to no good, the Bosnian Government side were up to no good, why were they corroborating these -- these reports that the shots came from their own territory, themselves? You think they might try and deny it, but that's just the first thing that occurs to me. Having said that, I mean, I can't -- I'm not going to attempt to comment further on it, because, as I say, I wasn't there and I have no knowledge of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were not in many places, and yet you voice your observations and conclusions about them. You just confirmed a little while ago that you received footages of many places that you, yourself, did not go to, and this is not a report of the Bosnian Government or their admission, this is an UNPROFOR conclusion. Can we now please see D680 in e-court. I would like to show you another of those reports, and there are many of them which, in a very responsible and serious manner, deal with the tricks played by the Muslim side during the war. Thank you. Can we please look at the third page. First of all, let's identify the document. This is a report of the United Nations, a technical report about the shelling in Livanjska Street on the 9th September 1994. Can we now move to the third page of the same document. We don't need the Serbian version. Thank you. It can be removed from the screen. Could you please look at the first and the last sentences of the conclusion. You can look at the entire conclusion, but let's not waste time. Could you please read aloud both of the sentences, if you don't mind?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which sentences do you want me to read? The last two? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first one and the last one, or, yeah, why not the whole conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay: "Conclusion: It is possible to conclude that the most suspected area --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "It is possible to conclude that the most suspected area are under the control of BiH."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see the utility of reading out all the passage. Could you read it and could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, this is another conclusion to the effect that the shell that nobody touched, just for your information, indicates that the shell had come from the Muslim side. There was another shell that had been moved, which made it suspicious or made the Serbs suspicious at having been fired at, but the one that wasn't touched or moved, showed clearly that it had come from the Muslim side. Were you aware of those reports or these kinds of reports?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of this report. And had I been in Sarajevo at the time, I would have been very interested in it and I would have tried to have done a story about it. No question about that. I have to say in my time there, I never saw anything like this, and it would have been newsworthy, of course. I don't know how many reports there are like this, but I'd be interested in seeing if there's anything like this in relation to any of the incidents that I reported on. But I'm not aware of anything like this, and I think the wider important point about the siege was that there was -- I mean, a war was going on. There was Serb shooting going into the city on a regular basis, which, as I said yesterday, I saw, and I saw the shell cases. But this particular thing, I mean, yeah, at the time it certainly would have made a story for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that. We'll see who opened fire and who shelled the city. This is a topic of its own. Do you know that from the first incident, which took place on the 27th May in the bread line in Vase Miskina Street, there was a serious suspicion among the UN representatives that the Muslim side was framing those incidents? If you had known that, would your paragraph 39 read differently, perhaps? All that time, the United Nations warned their officers and officials to be careful and to pay attention to the games to setting the scenes, to planting bodies, and this is what you heard as rumours. However, that was part of the official reports. If you'd known all that, would your paragraph 39 have suffered any changes?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, paragraph 39 says I heard it from an aide to UNPROFOR's General MacKenzie, but I never saw proof. And it's true, I never saw proof. So if there had been those kind of documents about the incidents on which I was reporting, I might have thought differently, but I haven't seen documents relating to the incidents on which I was reporting that sounded differently. But, you know, these are hypotheticals, so I can't really give you a particularly good answer on a hypothetical question. I prefer to stick to matters of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what about your reports of the incidents which you did not attend, and based on the visual, you came up with the textual part of the information? What about that? What are we supposed to think about those reports?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a different thing, sitting here in a courtroom 18 years on, trying to analyse a report about an incident which I wasn't at, to writing a story about an incident that occurred in the same part of the city where I was. I may not have been there precisely with my own eyes at that particular moment, but I was able quite often to go to the place in the aftermath and talk to people who were there and, therefore, absorb the context in which it happened. I don't think you can compare the two things at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you were aware of the war tricks that were played by the Muslim forces, and the goal of those tricks was to provoke an international intervention or to remove the Serbs from the scene; is that right? Were you aware of those political games on the part of the Muslim Army?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I repeat what I said before, that towards the end of my first stint in Sarajevo this aide to General MacKenzie spoke to me in an undertone, he sort of took me to one side and muttered about it as though he was passing on a very important secret, and of course I was intrigued by what he was saying and I looked for evidence of that. And after incidents, especially controversial incidents, you would often see soldiers doing crater analysis, but I don't remember them very often releasing the results of that. And I tend to think that had they found things which were -- which bore out the kinds of allegations that you are making, then perhaps it would have come out either then or since.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you in broader terms, not only about shooting at their own people, but at the tricks which were aimed at removing the Serbs from the scene. Let's look at another one of your reports. The number is 1D2928. Can this be shown, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Reporter: The war is coming closer to the UN Protection Force. Four Ukrainian soldiers were wounded when the radar battery they manned was attacked. They came under fire because Bosnian forces had mounted heavy guns 30 yards from their position. If the plan was to use them as a shield, it failed."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this one of those tricks that were played, moving one's own vehicles close to UNPROFOR installations and opening fire on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's very clear from the script what I reported at the time. They came under fire because Bosnian forces had mounted guns 30 yards from their position. If the plan was to use them as a shield, it failed. I mean, I reported it at the time. I don't see what the issue is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of the way various forces were deployed in Sarajevo? Were you aware of the whole picture?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly wasn't aware of any -- of the whole picture, no. I don't think anybody who was a journalist there was. The way that journalists work, I mean, we're people who essentially were on the outside, we're not insiders. I wasn't privy to the secret deliberations of the Bosnian Government. I wasn't privy to what you guys were doing in Pale. I wasn't privy to the secret discussions inside UNPROFOR. So certainly I didn't know the whole picture, no, of course not. As I said yesterday, as a reporter, all you can do is use your eyes and use your ears. You have to try and talk to people and find out what you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show another report of yours. 1D2931 is the number. And can the previous report be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D939, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce 1D2931.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: Territorials were moving to the front-line. Civilians whose homes they passed called out, May God protect you. "Jeremy Bowen, BBC News, Sarajevo. "Jeremy Bowen for NBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you at this location or did you receive a report from your cameraman?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, to be honest. It was such a short clip, I'd have to have a look at the whole piece and then maybe it would jog my memory. I mean, that's an eight-second clip from a piece I did 19 years ago. I really can't -- I mean, it's the first time I've seen it since I wrote those words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we have the number again? Did you say "1D2931"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, exactly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were there, and that could be seen from the entire footage. Now let me --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could I interrupt? I didn't see -- I also wasn't on the video screen fast enough to see the beginning of it. I just looked at the transcript. So was I there, was I in the picture? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that you were in the footage that precedes this particular clip. But, at any rate, it is your report. Let me ask you something now, Mr. Bowen. You, sitting in your hotel -- or if you were sitting in your hotel and if we were firing at these soldiers, how would you report this; that we were firing at the city, itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the witness got the message correctly. The transcript I have is a bit different from what is noted in the transcript. Can I read out the transcript from what I have? It says: "Two Bosnian territorials were moving up to the front-line. Civilians, whose homes they passed, were pulling up signs, May God protect you."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Had these young men been killed in this street, what would your report have said? Who were the Serbs firing at; civilians?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I probably wouldn't have said either. I would have -- I would have reported that they were young fighters who were moving up towards the front-line, who came under fire. I mean, I would have tried to report what happened. I would have said that had a shell landed at that particular moment right in the middle of them, and somehow miraculously the cameraman had escaped with the footage, I would have said, A group of fighters were moving up to the front-line when they came under fire and were killed. If they were civilians and if civilians had been killed, I would have said, Civilians who had been urging them on were also killed. I mean, the thing about it is I would try and report what happened. I mean, that's what I would have done. It seems quite straightforward to me. But, again, these are -- these are hypothetical questions about incidents that, in this case, didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I was going to interrupt before the witness gave the -- arguably, the only answer he could have given to a hypothetical question. It really doesn't assist us. It's much better if you can ask questions related to things which are factually indicated by the evidence, rather than going off on a hypothetical exercise, when the witness is bound to give you simply a hypothetical answer. Maybe an accurate answer and the essence of what he would have done in those circumstances, but how does that help anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, I agree. However, that's the impression you have because I haven't finished yet. I would like to draw the witness's attention to paragraph 24, and I would like you all to have a look at paragraph 24. You can see there, in paragraph 24 of his statement, that civilians had been trapped, in a way, or, rather, that a person can lose his or her life anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, it would have been different if you were present and if you saw a man carrying a rifle get shot. And imagine if somebody took away that rifle, and then you come to the conclusion eventually that it was civilians who got killed. So paragraph 24 of your statement implies that it was civilians who were targeted. I'm asking you the following: Are these young men a legitimate target?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's not for the witness to answer the question -- to answer such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, did the Muslims have an organised army in Sarajevo while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first was there in 1992, it was based on their Territorial Defence force, and it was a bit chaotic, I felt. They didn't have proper uniforms. There was some organisation, but it was more of a militia-type organisation, I'd say. By 1993, when General Delic was in charge, I'd say it was well organised, it started -- and then later in the war, it became -- it became better organised. I think as time went by, they -- in a military sense, they got their act together. I think at the beginning, though, in 1992, it was quite chaotic. For example, they relied on some charismatic individuals, some of whom were of dubious background, to organise some of their defence, whereas later on it was -- you could see that they were -- they were better armed, they had better uniforms, they had proper boots, and they responded more as a military formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bowen, did you know that the Muslim side, already in the spring of 1991, started organising its Patriotic League and that the Green Berets were some kind of an elite unit of that league? Did you know that when the war started, they had 120.000 to 150.000 troops in civilian clothing, but, nevertheless, well organised? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 150 -- I hadn't heard those figures before, no. I was aware that all sides had been -- had felt that war was coming and had been making some preparations. 1991, I have to say, I wasn't in Bosnia, except for one visit, and that was simply - I think I mentioned it yesterday - en route -- I was in Banja Luka en route to part of Croatia. My contact with former Yugoslavia in 1991 was covering the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did you hear of the Green Beret at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they had this -- the Green Berets, no, I didn't hear about the Green Berets. When I was there in 1992, there was a lot of talk about what they call the TOs or the Territorial Defence, I think, and I took that to be -- I understood that to be some kind of -- essentially, a militia force, not as -- not organised in a conventional military sense. I did know somebody who said he was involved in, quote/unquote, "special forces," but -- on the Bosnian Government side, but, you know, he was a young guy who had been in a military academy. So they weren't special forces in the sense that they would be special forces, say, in the US Army or the British Army or in the federal Yugoslav Army. So the Green Berets, no, I don't think I've heard that particular -- name of that unit or that -- it wasn't certainly being bandied around much or at all in my hearing when I was there in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, do you agree that at the beginning of August 1992, the entire Territorial Defence of Sarajevo, involving 500 different units, as reported by the president -- reported to the Presidency in mid-June by Sefer Halilovic, was brought together within the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did you know that the 1st Corps was in existence at the time, with about 15 brigades within the city itself?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that they were trying to organise themselves, because they didn't like -- there had been these guys who, I think, wore kind of black boiler suits, who ran around as part of their Territorial Defence, perhaps part of these 500 different units, and I know that they were trying to get them into proper uniforms and trying to organise themselves at that particular time. I didn't study the order of battle of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I have to admit, but I think the fact that if in -- if they had 500 different units to defend one not very big city, that suggests to me that -- by analysis, that it was a bit chaotic, was probably correct. But, as I say, they were definitely trying to organise, and the point I'm making is that by -- certainly by the following year, because I spent time talking to General Delic at his headquarters, they were definitely well organised by then. So that must have been when the process was beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you accept that the Muslim Army in Sarajevo had three times more personnel than the Sarajevo Romanija Corps? Please, if you could give shorter answers. Do you accept that the Muslim Army in Sarajevo had three times more personnel than the Sarajevo Romanija Corps already in 1992, from the very outset?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the Romanija Corps, you're referring to Bosnian Serb units. I have no idea how many personnel there were. I was struck, on my visits to the positions outside Sarajevo, that there weren't that many men that you could see in those four to five positions that you had going along, looking over the city. In terms of my knowledge of the Bosnian Serb units and armed forces, I was -- I was very struck by 1993 -- I was near Han Pijesak, and we bumped into a unit of very well organised Bosnian Serb -- I think they were some kind of mountain troops. They were very well equipped for winter warfare, they were very soldierly, if I might call it, very professional looking, and actually to a different calibre to many of the people I saw around Sarajevo, who seemed to be more like local guys. But, you know, I had the impression that that process of organisation was working on both sides, in terms -- you know, as war goes on, people get more organised and commanders come -- come to the fore. But as for precise numbers and orders of battle of the two opposing forces, I hadn't -- I wasn't privy to any of that kind of detail, I'm afraid. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw where Serb shells fell, and then you toured the locations from where Serb shells were being fired. Did you see where Muslim shells were falling, and did you tour the locations where they were being fired from, or, more precisely, do you know what kind of heavy weaponry, tanks, howitzers, mortars, the Muslim Army had within the city of Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely, but they clearly had some. And as time went by, they had more. They managed to obtain things. I didn't -- I did visit -- I'm trying to remember. I visited positions of the Bosnian Army around Sarajevo on the confrontation line. I managed to do that on a number of different occasions. It was -- as the war went on, it became harder to do that because they were reluctant to have people there. But, yes, I did visit them. I mean, I remember once -- in terms of positions, I remember once there was a recoilless rifle being used near the Holiday Inn, and we could hear it operating. There were -- there were exchanges of fire, yes, of course there were. There was a war going on. I mean, I was reporting it as a war. But, as I said, I'm trying -- the way I report was to try to look at their effect on civilians, because civilians in modern warfare suffer disproportionately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to show a few of your reports. Could we first have 1D2920, because this is what you say in paragraph 24: [In English] "Civilians were not caught in the cross-fire between the two warring armies." [Interpretation] Let us see what your reporting was at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: The UN convoy finally reached Sarajevo during a lull in the fighting. They soon found out why a UN official called this an all-out war. Shells and rockets started landing indiscriminately on people's homes. It wasn't clear who was doing the firing. There was less of it today, but no suggestion of a cease-fire."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems that, nevertheless, civilians had been trapped in this cross-fire between the two warring armies, right, and that, indeed, it is an all-out war, as you had heard from a UN official?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was quoting a UN official who was referring to that day, and I don't know what day -- I think it was 1992 again. I could have been more precise in my language in that paragraph, not quoting the cross-fire between two warring armies. I should have said something like "most of the time." When I was -- when I said that, what I was thinking of were the bodies I'd seen in the streets, killed by snipers, bodies of children, shells landing -- which I had seen landing myself in the city streets, where there were no military positions around. So one of the things that I used to do with colleagues to try to get some independent idea of the casualty levels was to visit the mortuary, and so we could -- you could get an idea from visiting the mortuary, because the bodies were in there, you know, clothed pretty much as they were when they came in, covered with dirt and muck and blood. They hadn't cleaned them up at all, and so if you looked in the mortuary, you could -- you could see whether they were fighters in uniform, with boots, with uniforms, you know, youngish men, or whether they were people who were clearly non-combatants, children, women, old people. And depending on the patterns that were going on, if the Bosnian Army had --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, Mr. Bowen. Please, let us try to be as brief and as expeditious as possible. This is your sentence: [In English] "Between 1992 and 1995, they were subject to an organised campaign of shelling and sniping by Bosnian Serb forces encircling the city." [Interpretation] Mr. Bowen, you have no basis for claiming that, and that's what I am trying to prove now. It's as if you were writing an indictment, and everything that you've been showing on the BBC says otherwise. Could this be admitted? Actually, can we admit all of it at the end, if that's easier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, could you answer his statement, rather than question, to the effect that the last word in para 24 is baseless?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not baseless, Your Honour. I would stand behind it 100 per cent. I think there was an organised campaign of shelling and sniping by Bosnian Serb forces encircling the city. I think it was aimed at putting pressure on the Bosnian Government. I think it was aimed at pressurising international opinion as well. I think it was a way of spreading terror among the population, and terror and cruelty and intimidating them. I think you could see that from the -- the way people died, the patterns of casualties, the fact that people were killed in their own houses. The reports -- I remember a report I did about children who were -- if I could just finish the sentence, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Don't interrupt the witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, I remember, for example, a story I did about a group of children who were killed when they were tobogganing. There was no military position near them. No parent in his right mind would allow their kids to toboggan near a military position during a war. It had been quite a quiet day, and a shell came on top of them and killed them. So that's what I based sentences like that on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we haven't dealt with the previous clip, which was rather short, 1D2931, and 1D2920. Do you have any objection to the admission of those two clips? They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits D940 and D941 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, with all due respect, I will have to ask for additional time if your answers continue to be this extensive. Now I'm going to ask you the following: A shell fell close to some children. Do you have any proof of that being a Serb shell? On the basis of what do you say that or are you relying on your feelings, on your emotions? Do you have any proof that that was a Serb shell?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes or no? There is no reason to go beyond that. Yes or no, do you have any proof?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you can't limit the witness like that. If you ask an open question that is perhaps going to lead to a series of explanations, then you have to live with it. If the witness can answer the question expeditiously, he will, but he needs to answer it in the way that actually provides the best evidence he can give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Morrison. Yes, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My belief that the Serbs were besieging the city and that their shells killed a lot of the -- killed the people who were killed is based on the fact that I spent months there. At times, you could see the muzzle flashes of weapons as they fired coming into the city, you could see the impacts. I went around the positions and I saw the empty shell cases. I spoke to people on the positions who told me about how they fired on the city. I saw dead bodies with bullets in their heads, and so on, of civilians. And that is what I would base it on. And I think in that particular report about the tobogganing children, I didn't give any -- I mean, I don't have the script in front of me and it was 18 or 19 years ago. I don't -- I don't remember exactly what form of words I used, but I'm sure it was accurate, subject to the information that I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I cannot go into that, who you got that information from. That requires an investigation, Mr. Bowen. Tell me, did Muslims fire from the city, sometimes perhaps even more than the Serbs who were firing at the city; yes or no? That's easy enough for you.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims fired from the city. The Muslim side did fire from the city. Of course, a war was going on. In terms of overall fire-power, my feeling always was that the Serbs had greater fire-power, and they were also firing from elevated positions, which gave them a definite military advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you believe that Muslims did not have their own positions on the hills and that they did not have any artillery and mortars on the hills around Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The witness simply didn't say that. You're attributing words and opinions to him that were not indicated. It's not helping anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellency, a great deal remains unclear. How is it that Mr. Bowen can say that anything that is firing from the hills at the city is Serb weaponry rather than Muslim weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or, Mr. Bowen, when you see casings, can you recognise whether they were fired at legitimate targets or civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the casings, no. But I could see where the targets were by where they landed. You know, the numbers of people -- a tank shell went through the apartment of my translator's family, for example. That wasn't a military position, and it wasn't fired from inside the city. So I could see where these shells were landing and I could see, when I went up there, that they had been fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Muslims have any tanks in town, and did you report about that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw tanks moving. I saw some wrecked tanks. Maybe they had some tanks. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D2923.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Bowen, your colleague, Martin Bell, established here, and that could be seen from his report as well, that there were days when the Muslims fired a great deal more from the town at the Serbs, as compared to the Serbs firing at the city, so that is what his reports also said. Could we have this video played now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was there a question about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the question would come after we see this video together. Is that the case, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, thank you. Can we have the video played.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: The Muslims direct quite a lot of fire at these Serbian positions high above Sarajevo, but they're well neigh impregnable."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The clip being so short, I'm not sure whether we can follow the context. But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I can probably explain what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were aware of that, and you even reported about that, that the Serb positions around Sarajevo were subjected to heavy fire coming from the city itself. Now I'm asking whether you know that Mr. Martin Bell confirmed here and also said, in his own reports at the time, that often more fire came from the city than into the city.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking your points one by one: I didn't see Martin Bell's testimony here, and I haven't read it either, so I don't know what he said to you and to the Court. Of course, there were -- I mean, I don't think at any point today or yesterday or in my reporting I ever denied that the Bosnian -- I'm not trying to suggest that they were people who had no weapons and weren't firing. A war was going on, and they were trying to fire, no doubt, as much as they could. The point I was making in that very short extract that you played was that, yes, they received heavy fire at times, not all the time, because I was standing there and it wasn't happening at that particular moment, but they had impregnable -- well neigh impregnable positions. I mean, they were -- an up-hill assault against them by infantry, I would say, would have been impossible, given that they had no air support and so on. So they were -- what I was trying to say was, yes, they received fire, but they were able to continue with what they were doing and were able to hunker down and resist any of those assaults. A war was going on there. Both sides were firing. Of course that was the case. I don't think I've ever suggested anything to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the Court please produce 1D2924. That's another one of your reports.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: Serbian command was attacked at about 4.30 this morning. They fought their way into an area called Skenderija, close to a building which houses the Muslim Presidency. After about an hour of heavy fighting, either they withdrew or they were pushed out. It's impossible to tell which."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fighting is going on in the very center of Sarajevo here; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, near to the Presidency, I was saying in that piece. You could also hear -- on the soundtrack, you could hear incoming bullets as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the following report, can we have it? Or maybe this one can be admitted first, so maybe it can be admitted later. Shall we have it admitted now or later, the whole series?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll deal with one by one. I take it there's no position, Ms. Edgerton. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, they're actually so brief that I'm really at a loss as to any context for this. They're seconds. We don't know when, we don't know where, we don't know place, we don't know surrounding events in any regard. It makes it not only difficult for the witness to give any kind of useful comment for the Chamber, but, I think, difficult for all of us to understand its utility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. While I understand your point, and to a certain degree I agree with you, but given that the witness was able to explain the context, we'll proceed admitting these two clips.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits D942 and D943, Your Honours, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please see the following report. The number is 1D2926. We don't have any time for any longer reports. I would love to show them, but unfortunately the time's too short.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: Nobody here expects a short war. They won't starve as long as it's UN brings in food, but the only safe thing they can do is stay in their cellars, thinking about a different life, still hoping they'll be saved by foreign troops. "Heavy exchanges of artillery and tank fire. Mortars and machine guns disturbed them again last night. Everybody here expects the same tonight. "Jeremy Bowen, BBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, you report about heavy exchanges of artillery and tank fire; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we not see this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We saw it in its entirety yesterday. I'm just trying to find the reference in the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I make one point --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, it's not necessary, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I make one point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a reporter, it's quite hard to make out, sometimes, which fire is coming from where, but you do have some clues. With tank fire, there's a different kind of sound when it arrives and when it goes out. And if the point that you're making is both sides were firing tanks at each other, I heard sounds coming in. I didn't hear that characteristic sound of a tank fire going out, though; certainly not on that piece, as I was listening to that soundtrack there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say in this report that there was heavy fighting in Sarajevo, including exchanges of artillery and tank fire? Did you say this in your report? I believe I heard your words to that effect in your report.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and by that, what I meant was there was generalised exchanges and it was quite difficult to say what was happening at different times. I mean, I was -- I was in my hotel room, listening to it. It was in the middle of the night. It was very loud, I think, on that particular day. But, yes, exchanges of fire, certainly artillery and tank fire. I was just trying to offer a little bit more context about what I heard, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was P2074 yesterday, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have another one before the break, 1D02930. Or perhaps two before the break, because they're both very short. Apologies. 1D02927 is the correct number, 1D2927.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: Last night's fighting was the heaviest for seven weeks. Military objectives are hard to assess here, but it seems that the Muslims, who hold the city center, attacked Serb positions. Croats were then drawn into the fighting, but it's not clear on which side. Tanks, heavy artillery and mortars fired hundreds of rounds during what became an inclusive battle."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It arises from your words that there is equality on both sides, that both sides are equal, and the Muslim side has just launched an offensive?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, if I could just clarify that, looking at the transcript. I don't think I'm suggesting there was equality on both -- if you're trying to imply that there was always equality on both sides, I don't think that was the case. But they certainly could launch offensives. Their problem was sustaining them. They were quite good at launching them for, you know, a night or something like that. The difficulty was holding on to what territory they were able to get and following it up and holding that territory. I had connections with some people who were fighters, who would tell me they'd take their initial objectives, then resupply wouldn't arrive, and then they'd fall back with casualties. I mean, that was a repeated pattern. But certainly they could mount offensives, and in 1995 they were getting more ambitious in trying to do that. 1992, rather less so, because they didn't have the capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more. 1D2930, as the best illustration of what we are talking and also set the base for a new explanation of the military policy that was pursued in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Reporter: Fighting went on all night in and around Sarajevo. In the last few days, there'd been some of the most bitter battles of the war. During the night, heavy rain fell on the city. Usually, that's about the only thing that stops the killing. It didn't last night. It appears that the Bosnian Government's forces are throwing most of what they have left at the Serbs. By dawn, it was clear they were getting it back with interest. For more than an hour this morning, there were more than 15 powerful explosions every minute."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, Mr. Bowen, when I say this is another proof that at the time you fully understood that there was a war going on, and that that night the Muslim forces had launched an offensive that night, and that by then it was clear that they were getting it back with interest, as you say?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's what I said in the piece.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, and then we'll continue talking about the last report and deal with the military policy in town. Can the two clips be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits D944 and D945 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into, briefly, private session before we rise for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, you said it yourself, that the main area of interest for you was the suffering of civilians, and I respect that. When you said that, did you mean both Serbian and Muslim civilians, in other words, civilians on both sides of the front-line?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that there were between 60.000 and 70.000 Serbs living in Sarajevo under the Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there continued to be Serbs there during the war as well. I know that because I was friendly with some. The issue that we had with trying to cover both sides of the war was that access on the Serb side, especially, was very difficult. It was very hard to get permission to go to places we wanted to go. For example, I was only able to visit Grbavica once in the entire war, despite repeated requests at the press office in Pale to do so. Had we been able to operate as freely on your side as on the Bosnian Government side, we would have been able to cover both sides far more effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 27 in your statement, where you speak about the same matter, but you make a slight distinction and you say that Serbs had it a bit easier because they had access to decent food and had a way out; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's correct. When I used to go even to Lukavica, and certainly when I went to Pale, we would buy food in Pale to take back into Sarajevo for our own personal consumption. You could get decent food there, you could get good Serbian beer, you could have a good meal at a restaurant. It was -- you know, for us, to be honest, visiting Pale was -- was always a little bit of a holiday, or Jahorina. I used to always enjoy going there. And I saw once -- for example, while I was there in Jahorina, I saw the ski championships going on of the Bosnian Serb military, so the ski lifts were operating for that particular day. You know, so -- and the other point I could take away from my one visit, and I admit it was one visit to Grbavica, was that hardly anybody was living there. The vast majority of people had left. There were one or two old couples who had clearly been reluctant to leave their homes, but there weren't any young people. I didn't see any kids, I didn't -- life wasn't going on there. It was essentially, it seemed to me, a ghost town with some military positions in there and one or two elderly people who had been reluctant to get out. There was a much bigger hinterland on the Bosnian Serb side, where people could go out and continue with lives which were a little bit -- which were more normal than the kinds of lives that people had within the confrontation lines in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just going to ask you whether you saw or knew about the conditions of Serbs in Ilidza, in Ilijas, in Lukavica, and in Nedzarici, especially those who were circled from three and a half sides, and Grbavica, that you described just a minute ago yourself. Do you agree that people suffered badly there, as well as the 70.000 Serbs did under the Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was suffering on both sides of the line. I think the lines -- I think the suffering inside the confrontation lines was worse. There's no question that some of the Serbs who were inside Sarajevo had a tough time because of their ethnicity. However, there were others there who I met who said that they believed in a multicultural way of life and were happy to be there and didn't want to get out. Well, didn't want to get out to Srpska, anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D2929, another of your reports which has been admitted, just to jog your memory and then continue along the same line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: Going down the wrong street at the wrong time of day in Sarajevo can kill you. Last week, a group of men on the Serbian side of the line set out to deliver bread and sardines to the front. It seemed quiet enough, but a sniper saw them and shot one of them through the head. The sniper went on firing. They wanted to drag the body away, but they didn't have a rope, so they used a hose instead. "In only four months, shelling, sniping, and the grim business of dealing with what they do to human beings has become part of the everyday routine here on both sides of the lines. People are forced to exist around it."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems that at the time, you had a balanced approach to both sides when you reported, and you said that people suffered on both sides. You confirmed that for us just a while ago. And, in any case, I just wanted to jog your memory and I just wanted to confirm that your position was that what was going on in Sarajevo was a war, due to which the civilian population on both sides suffered; right? And I'm talking about the population on both sides of the front-line.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that there was an equality of suffering, no, if that's what you're trying to say. I think that it was worse inside the confrontation lines than on the Bosnian Serb side. You'll recall that in that piece that you just played part of, the bit that came before that, was the man called Kujundzic, burying his entire family, pretty much, including children, and he had been safe because he had left the place where they were sheltering to watch the news and the shell came in while -- sorry, listening to news on the radio. So in that piece -- I mean, that piece actually encapsulates it quite well. He was a man who was shot taking supplies up to the Bosnian Serb soldiers and their positions on one side. On the other side, there was a family sheltering from the shelling, killed in the shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The next document I would like to present to the witness is 1D2933.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This man, Kujundzic, as far as you know, was he a Serb? Is this a Serb family name, a Serb first name?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You tell me. I don't know what his ethnicity was, but the fact was he was in -- inside the city, and he was line in the Lion's Cemetery, and we came upon him quite by chance. I think I'd been up to the hospital, we were driving past, and I saw a big earth-works going on where a whole lot of people were digging a whole lot of graves. So as a reporter, I was curious. We stopped and got out, and through the translator, I spoke to the guy, and he told me his story, which was in the piece which I think we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at the video that I have just called.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: On the other side of the city, nearly a thousand people, mainly mothers and children, became refugees this morning. Almost all of them were Serbs. Until the war started, they'd lived happily enough alongside Muslims and Croats." "Horrible, horrible. I have to go. This is my town, I'm born here, and my child born here, and my father living here. I have to leave everything." "Reporter: Misery is about the only thing the ordinary people of the former Yugoslavia still have in common. "Jeremy Bowen, BBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was your question about this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just going to ask Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the people who were born in Sarajevo, who lived in Sarajevo, 157.000 Serbs and 23.000 Yugoslavs, of whom 20.000 were probably Serbs, because Muslims and Croats did not declare themselves as Yugoslavs at that time, did they -- they all wanted to stay, and they couldn't, and that's why they were crying. Were they refugees in their own city, as you stated it yourself, and do you -- are you sure that many of them wanted to stay? Do you know that the Serbs were not allowed to leave Sarajevo, as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the report was quite clear about what was going on on that particular occasion. I was always glad to do stories like that, when they came up, because I think it was clear that Serbs were having a hard time. And as the war went on, they had a harder time within the city itself. I don't think there's any dispute about that. And I -- in none of my reporting did I ever suggest that one side were angels and the other side worked with devils. What I suggested was a war was going on, and the way it worked out was that the civilian population that suffered most, that I came across, were people who were besieged in Sarajevo, compared to the people around Sarajevo. Also, in other besieged places, I saw suffering, too, in the course of the war. But as I've said, a war was going on, it was a very tough situation, and hard things happened on all sides. My feeling was that the preponderance of suffering was inflicted -- in that particular part of the theatre was inflicted on the people within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 1D291D [as interpreted]. And before we do that, could the previous one be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The 1D2933 will be admitted as Exhibit D946. And I take it the previous one to that, the 1D2929, was the one we saw yesterday, which was admitted as P2077.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. The following document is 1D2919. Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, you, yourself, witnessed the suffering of the Serbs in Sarajevo. They lived in cellars, where they sought shelter from the shelling; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the thing about shelling in an urban area is shelling doesn't discriminate. It doesn't matter what -- where you came from, where you were a Serb, Croat, Bosnian, British, French. If you're in the wrong place at the wrong time and a shell came in, then you get hurt or killed. So, yes, of course, if you're in an area where they are shelling, of course you take shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In my question, something was not recorded. The Serbs on the Serb side, in the Serbian part of Sarajevo. Can that be inserted? And now can we please look at --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I didn't answer that question, though. I didn't hear "Serbian part of." As I said, I only -- it was very hard to visit the Serb side of Sarajevo, and I only went once to Grbavica, so it's very hard for me to make the kind of judgements about that place that I could make about the Bosnian Government-controlled parts of the city, where I -- of which I was very familiar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now watch the following video-clip, and you will tell us where you recorded that, on what part -- or, rather, on what side of the front-line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: Any talk of cease-fires in this war should be treated with great caution. It will take much more than that to coax Sarajevo's civilians out of their cellars. These women are Serbs. They've boon underground for two months. A few streets away, Muslims live in just the same way. The fighting resumed today, killing at least 11 more people. The leader of the Bosnian Serbs, Radovan Karadzic, perhaps on the orders of the beleaguered Belgrade government, said it was time to stop." "Radovan Karadzic: We unilaterally announce a cease-fire from Monday, June the 15th, 1992, at 6.00 p.m. We also request a substantial pause of at least 800 officers of the UN peacekeeping forces to monitor from Serbian positions this cease-fire." "Reporter: Today in Sarajevo, Serbian gunmen were patrolling their territory. For the first time, their leader says they'll let UN monitoring into their positions." "This is policeman Serbia." "Reporter: If they follow his orders, they could make the UN's job easier. If the Muslims and the Croats stop attacking as well, the UN will try to reopen the airport to bring in much-needed relief supplies."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This was 1D2919.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, do you know that this was not the first offer of a unilateral cease-fire, there were offers even before that, but you were not there? On the 22nd of April, there was a well-known Serbian platform on a cease-fire and on the non-recognition of the fait accompli. Do you know that this was not the first time that we offered or tabled a unilateral cease-fire, not the first time or the last time either? There were many attempts on our side to introduce a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to -- I'm just looking back through the script there. I don't think it was the first offer, did I? Also, I'd like to make the point, the 15th of June, I was in London. That piece was put together with agency pictures in London. I wasn't in the Balkans at the -- at that time. I don't think I went to Sarajevo until July, it was not until July, and I flew in on one of the early flights that came in. So I wasn't in the city when that particularly happened, but I would have done that piece based on wire service reports, mainly. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the monitor in front of you tell you that it was 12th of June that it was broadcast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, but he says in his statement from the 12th of June, were offering it, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 15th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 15th, was it? Yeah, I mean, what I heard him mentioning the date in that clip, it was June, and I wasn't there in June. That's the point I was making, that's all, because before he played it, Dr. Karadzic said that -- he was asking where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can explain. On the 12th of June, we held a press conference, and the offer was for a cease-fire to be introduced on the 15th of June. That's when we were supposed to introduce the cease-fire and stop fighting, and that's the difference in dates. Thank you. I'm not going to ask you, then, that on the 8th of June a large Muslim offensive was launched in Sarajevo. And can we now look at 1D2921, which is another of your reports. And before that, can the previous report be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D947, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For your information only, Mr. Bowen, it was not the Government of Serbia who gave me any orders. They were not in a position to give me any orders. There were constant tensions about that. That was our genuine offer.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it a question or are you just making a statement, which is unacceptable? Do you like to comment on that, Mr. Bowen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd like to thank Dr. Karadzic for the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Reporter: Today, the UN took a convoy of food to --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was only to satisfy Mr. Bowen's curiosity, so he does not need to wonder, he does not need to go on wondering about things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's not waste time. Shall we try again from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Reporter: ... Grbavica, a suburb of Sarajevo now controlled by Bosnians. But Bosnians who have no sympathy for the UN's even-handed approach who want active military support instead accuse the peacekeepers of smuggling weapons to the Serbs and stop them crossing their lines." "Reception is as important as reality in Sarajevo, and therefore it was important to go through the front door, through the presidential positions into an area within Sarajevo. That failed miserably two times." "Reporter: In the end, the food got in through the back door, via Serbian territory. The civilians liked it but the failure of the convoy's symbolic purpose shows the warring factions and the UN are as far apart as ever. The UN commander says his relations with the Bosnians are at an all-time low."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, in this clip you confirmed that the Muslim side did not allow UN to transport food across their territory to the Serbian part of the central part of Sarajevo, Grbavica. Do you know that all the Muslims received, on the other hand, was transported across the Serbian territory, and they, in their turn, would not allow us to receive just one convoy through their territory?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I -- I didn't report the other thing on that piece, at least not in that snippet, but I -- that's what I reported, that the Muslim -- their government were making it difficult for the UN to take things through. That was in the piece very clearly, I thought.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D948, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Without wanting to attack you, I just want to be precise. I just want to be very precise when talking about your reports. Do you know that it was -- do you think that it was very important for you to know where the facilities of the BiH Army were in the city of Sarajevo? Was that needed for you to establish whether their targets were legitimate?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the targeting policy of the BiH Army is to do with where -- is to do with what they shoot at, not where they shoot from, necessarily. Driving around Sarajevo at that particular time, I have to say that one would see, actually, very few weapons, very few personal weapons, very few AK-47s. There unquestionably were BiH Army positions, where they had heavier weapons, but they were all pretty well hidden, because I was -- apart from I saw a few heavier mortars and so on at front-line positions, I certainly never saw things, positions -- I'm not saying they weren't there, but I never saw positions in obvious places in populated parts of the city. One thing that struck me -- after Bosnia, I went to the Middle East, and it really struck me strongly, and I put this in a BBC report once, that at the Jerusalem Bus Station, on the Friday night when reserve soldiers were going home, you'd see more automatic weapons than you'd see in people walking down the streets in down-town Sarajevo in the middle of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to look at your paragraph 33 in your statement, where you say that there were some parts of town which were shelled more often than others: [In English] "but generally the pattern was random." [Interpretation] And then you say another thing which the Defence cannot accept. You say this: [In English] "Bosnian Serb forces knew where things were. They could just lob shells in." [Interpretation] Did you ever hear of mobile mortars on cars, on lorries, that circled Sarajevo and opened fire on the Serb positions there?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard or saw mobile positions on the backs of lorries, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
