utterances.text: Thank you. That's a well-known fact here by now. In paragraph 52, you say: [In English] "The siege of Sarajevo was one of the most straightforward facts of a complicated war. I used to feel that a lot of the diplomacy was based on wishful thinking and fiction. In my view, the Western powers were not well informed about what was happening." [Interpretation] Do you believe that in Sarajevo, there were no secret services, both military and civilian secret services, from all countries, Albania included, and do you really think that the governments didn't know what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I based that on conversations I had with British government ministers. I remember one visited Sarajevo and I was astounded by his ignorance. No doubt intelligence services were operational, but I think one of the lessons I've taken away in my time as a foreign correspondent, especially the last 10 years or so, is that intelligence services are not infallible and often know very little or get it wrong. My strong feeling was -- I mean, you take, for example, the London Conference in 1992. After speaking to some of the people who were involved in setting it up, I knew it was going to fail, because it was based on some wishful thinking and ignorance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D2936, can we see that now, please. It's another one of your reports.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Serbs are around various positions in the city. They are containing the area from any military break-out by the Bosnians. I'm just not using the word 'siege.'" "Reporter: He preferred to say 'strategic encirclement.'" "You call it siege of Sarajevo. We are talking that they are in tactical advantageous positions around the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, now we are coming to the point -- actually, you said this in one of your reports, and now we're going to see which one it was. Actually, we saw it a few moments ago. You said it was hard to assess what military targets were, what military targets were in Sarajevo, and you said that in your report. 2927: [In English] "Military objectives are hard to assess here." [Interpretation] Let me ask you this, Mr. Bowen: Do you agree that it was a bit excessive on your part to disagree with the United Nations and their characterisation of the military situation in Sarajevo? They said, and that was the official position, that it was not a siege, but rather a containment, containment of the entire 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to prevent a breakthrough; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a siege. For political reasons in that particular year, they tried to vary their language. And that poor, hapless Canadian spokesman there, who was a nice man, Barry Frewer, lost his job as a result of trying to come up with a form of words that was plainly nonsensical, which was widely ridiculed, and they dropped that insistence very shortly afterwards, and he was the main victim of it. I base my view that it was a siege not on statements defining it by officials, but by what I saw, myself, about the fact that there were thousands of people there who were stuck, couldn't get out, and who were at the mercy of people who were attacking, and that the war was going on and fighting was going out as well. It was a war going on. A city was encircled and put under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was it that lived in Serb-controlled territories, Mr. Bowen?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina or around the city?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You may put it that way as well, but now we're talking about Sarajevo. Did Serbs control a single Muslim neighbourhood in Sarajevo or did they only control neighbourhoods that were predominantly Serb populated, suburbs of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the war I think they were predominantly Serb populated, but I spoke to plenty of people who lost their homes in the outlying districts of Sarajevo, who were Muslims, who had moved into the center of the city when life became impossible for them on the -- in the places where they lived; for example, the vast majority of the people who were in the Europa Hotel, who were people who -- Muslims who'd been displaced from Serb-controlled parts of Sarajevo, in the main.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, it's easy for us to prove, on the basis of the census, that Serb-controlled territories were predominantly Serb, over 80 or 90 per cent Serb. Do you have that knowledge or do you have proof to the contrary? In Sarajevo, the Serb forces controlled Serb neighbourhoods. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have to take your word for that. I don't have the -- I don't have access to the census to which you refer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So at one point in your statement, you say that the Serbs did not want to or could not take new parts of the city. Now, I have to find that, but I will manage to do so. Now we are talking military politics in the zone of Sarajevo. Did the Muslims want to take Serb-held parts of town, and did they try to do that? What was the point of their offensives all over the place?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes, it wasn't clear what they were trying to do when they mounted an offensive. I think they were -- from the military point of view, my analysis was that for the Serb side to try to take the city would have been a very ambitious project, would have involved street-fighting, which is a very difficult thing to do, requiring a lot of men, and my assessment at the time, thinking back on it, was that your side was well equipped, in terms of fire-power, in terms of heavy weapons, but you weren't able or didn't feel able to mount the kind of sustained ground assault that would have taken the city. And perhaps the conclusion -- and I wasn't privy to your discussions, but perhaps the conclusion that you took was that it wasn't necessary to do that and you didn't want to do that, but that's -- that's not something which I can comment on because I wasn't -- as I say, I'm not qualified to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that once we could no longer take the attacks from Otes, we took Otes? When we decided to take Otes, we did so. Otes is a neighbourhood near Ilidza. We did take what we wanted to take. Our military policy in Sarajevo was the containment of forces and awaiting a political solution. Do you know that we took Otes?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that you took Otes. I knew some of the people who were involved in the fighting there of the Bosnian Government side. No, I think I was trying to say that in the last answer, that besieging the city was clearly, for you, what you believed to be an appropriate tactic, in my opinion at the time and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now make a distinction between two different things. This is what I'm putting to you: The containment of 70.000 to 80.000 Muslim soldiers of the 1st Corps is a legitimate objective of the Serb Army, whereas keeping civilians in the town of Sarajevo was not our policy. We weren't the ones who were keeping civilians in Sarajevo. Do you agree that it was the Muslim government that prevented the free movement of civilians? It wasn't the Serb side that kept asking for people to be allowed to leave. We even organised the organisation of Slovenes, Jews. We were always there at people's service so that they could be evacuated, while the Muslim government was carrying out an internal siege in relation to civilians.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they were carrying out an internal siege, I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I have 1D2913 for a moment. It's a UN document. 1D2913 in e-court for a moment. No, it's not a broadcast. It's a document. Oh, perhaps it doesn't have to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It wasn't yet up-loaded. In the meantime, shall we admit the previous clip, 1D2936? That will be admitted as Exhibit D949.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would appreciate that. Thank you. Could this please not be broadcast, except for the participants in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please cast a glance at this. It is a report dated the 17th of August, 1994, and it involves highest-ranking officials of the UN in Sarajevo. And you see, at the very bottom, that it involves a meeting with this general in Sector Sarajevo. Can we now have a look at the next page. Let's not mention any names. The participants saw the names. Could you please look at number 2 of this report: [In English] "The BiH government seemed to present the international community with propaganda regarding violations committed by the Serb side, omitting to do the same regarding violations committed by them. "For example, the civilian population has major administrative obstacles in leaving Sarajevo, and the police and military officials, being powerful, contribute significantly to this policy." [Interpretation] Do you believe these high-ranking officers of the UN?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to read through the document. Sorry. Well, I believe that this is a document from high-ranked officers of the UN and officials of the UN, giving their opinions and analysis of the time, yeah. Obviously, that's what the document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Had you been aware of this document at the time, would you have come to realise that the siege that pertained to civilians was imposed by the Muslim side, and whereas encirclement that had to do with military matters was imposed by the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one fed off the other. I mean, my view of that, I know that people couldn't -- I'm trying to -- sorry, I'm hesitating because I'm just trying to get -- it's been a while since I've thought of these things and discussed them. I'm trying to think back to what my understanding was at the time. I mean, yes, if I'd got that document, it would have made a very interesting story, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I mean, yes -- I mean, I didn't have the document, so I can't really comment on what -- about it at the time, except that I would have been glad to have had it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D950, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Actually, this document I don't believe is subject to any kind of restrictions, and it has been publicly filed as part of our 30th motion for disclosure violations, Annex A to that, so I don't think there's any need to have it under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Can I get confirmation from you, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, when you saw Mr. Reid roll his chair over to me, he had just received information to that effect, updating the information that I had. So my friend is completely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted publicly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have a look at 1D2922. It's another one of your reports from the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You do remember that as regards that report of yours of the 15th of June, I invited the UN to observe Serb artillery positions around Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that as a result of that 15th of June offer, you made that offer, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have a look at it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: This Serbian battery is one of the sprinkling of positions at which the UN is able to station monitors full time." "Everybody can hide something, but I think on the positions, the co-operations with the local commanders is very good, so I think we are in control of everything on the positions. This does not mean that we control every weapon around Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This officer of the UN is praising co-operation with local commanders. We made them an offer to the effect of observing each and every one of their position. However, they didn't have enough personnel. Are you aware of that, they simply did not have enough personnel to observe all of these positions, so we had to group our weapons within certain groups, nine, eleven --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That quite wasn't quite what he was saying in the piece. And my impression of the activities of the UN Military Observers, the UNMOs at the time, was that they had a certain number of positions and they could vouch for what was happening within their -- within their line of sight, essentially. And they had some fairly primitive equipment to monitor things going up as well. But what they would always say, and I had many conversations with them, was that the places where they weren't, they couldn't vouch for what was happening because they weren't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, this is sometime in the summer of 1992. Do you know that after that, in order to enable them to observe our artillery, although they did not have enough personnel, we grouped our weaponry at nine positions, at the most, so that they could observe all of our weapons? These were these so-called weapon collections under UN supervision.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware at the time of that, no. I wasn't aware of it until now, that you had formal groups of positions. That's certainly something that didn't come out into the journalistic community in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I accept that criticism of our PR capability. It is correct that we did not manage to present our case properly. However, no matter what kind of military knowledge or education you have, do you agree, Mr. Bowen, that this kind of grouping of weaponry jeopardises our military position and that it would have been better if they had more personnel so that they could monitor each and every one of our positions, rather than having us group our weapons at nine positions only?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really answer that question because I don't know whether you had any other weapons that weren't in those groups that were being observed. I think that the point that the UNMOs made was they knew what was going on where they were, but they didn't know what was going on in other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you accept that it only depended on them, whether they would observe a particular position or not; it was their lack of manpower rather than anything we did to stop them from doing so?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea about what kind of manpower they had there. Certainly, UNMOs working around Sector Sarajevo who I spoke to were generally quite pleased with co-operation that they had, but they had -- as I say, they constantly said their problem was they couldn't be in all places at all times, so they could only look at a certain snap-shot of the war and not the whole picture.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before that happens, Your Honour, maybe it's helpful if I note that this is another very brief excerpt of the same film that D942 is drawn from, and maybe, administratively, they could be somehow linked. Not the same film; "same report" is what I meant to say, the same broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 2923 -- 24 -- D2 -- 942 was something that was very short.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This clip, which I think is D2922, is drawn from the same broadcast that is -- what i D2923, which has now been marked as D942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So with that explanation, we can admit separately this 2922; is that your suggestion? Thank you. So this will be admitted as Exhibit D951.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll go back to Sarajevo, at least as far as certain aspects are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we're dealing with that part of Gorazde, let me say this: At paragraph 55, you say that you arrived at Gorazde and the streets were empty, and so on and so forth. Do you remember that? Could you have a look at that paragraph of your statement? It's number 55.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, you say in paragraph 60 that you did not stay there for a long time, that you did not see much of the city, but that you did see a lot of artillery damage. Are you suggesting, by way of these paragraphs, that it was the Serbs who were attacking Gorazde, that was an unprotected city, an unarmed city, that they were attacking unarmed civilians, or are you saying that the Muslim Army is stationed in Gorazde and that they were the first to start every bit of fighting in and around Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying was that there was a war going on there, that there was fighting happening; of course there was. I think I made that clear in the report that was shown to the Court yesterday. And that there were many civilians who were there also and who were, as a result of the war, besieged in the town.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 1D2925. Actually, I don't know whether we saw that yesterday. We have to decide now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Bowen, how many Serbs lived in Gorazde in the beginning of 1992 and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at this report now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: The UN convoy was only 10 kilometres from Gorazde when it was ambushed. Muslim guerrillas are harassing Serbian regulars in this part of Eastern Bosnia, but it isn't clear who carried out the attack. An armoured personnel carrier and a UN lorry ran over land-mines. Small-arms fired which followed forced the expedition to turn back."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this confirms what you had said a moment ago. At the time, you were aware of the fact that Muslim guerrillas, as you call them, constantly attacked Serb regulars around Gorazde; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- it's not quite clear from that short snippet where that incident took place. I think that was the previous attempt to get into Gorazde before the one -- the successful attempt that I was on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have a look at this. Let us see what the views of top-ranking UN officials are with regard to Gorazde. Could we show Mr. Bowen D686 so that he sees what General Sir Michael Rose says about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, Mr. Bowen: Why did you not show us all this extensive damage that you saw before getting to Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that I saw damage inside Gorazde, not getting into Gorazde. The route that we took was -- coming up to the town was in a -- was a rural area, so there weren't things too damaged. Inside the town, there was quite a bit of damage, and we showed some of it. Our time was very limited there, and we spent a lot of time -- well, a lot of the limited time that we had trying to get a range of pictures to try, as best we could, to illustrate the situation inside Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to tell you that yesterday you just showed a smashed window, and your cameraman was filming the street from there. Let's now see what General Rose says. How could you distinguish between Serb houses that had been destroyed or torched and Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you can distinguish between houses that have been shelled and houses that have been smashed up by individuals. And I certainly couldn't distinguish -- I had no idea who owned individual houses.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Reporter: ... flew by helicopter into Gorazde following the fighting, Rose was asked about US satellite reports that nearly every house in Gorazde was damaged." "Yes, practically every house in Gorazde has been damaged, but most of the damage to Gorazde was done in the fighting that had taken place some two years before, when the Bosnian Government forces drove the Serbs from this town, and there were 12 and a half thousand Serbs at that time living here, and they were all driven off. The way to distinguish a house that has been damaged by fighting where a shell has hit it, and a house that has been damaged by ethnic cleansing, is if its got no roof, no doors, no window frames, nothing in the house at all, and there are burn marks up it and bullets spread around the walls, that is a house that's damaged by ethnically cleansing. The house that has been damaged by shelling has a shell hole in it and there are still people trying to live in that building with their furniture in it because they've got nowhere else to go. That is damage you can't see from satellite. And, of course, at that time the international image of what had happened in Gorazde was very different from the reality. What was dangerous was that policy that was going to be put together on both sides of the Atlantic about what we should do in Gorazde, but these policies were being put together on totally flawed information."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I'm waiting for the interpretation to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would it have been useful for you if you'd been aware of this report? I believe that the report did air on BBC. I don't know who made it. It may have been Mr. Bell. Were you aware of the testimony of the 12.500 Serbs in Gorazde, about their suffering at the very outset of the war?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I said yesterday that there was ethnic cleansing carried out by all sides in the wars of the former Yugoslavia. As for respective -- different amounts of damage, I think I said in my last answer, to my previous answer, that you can distinguish between houses that have been smashed up by individuals and houses that have been shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, the Defence does not recognise an even-handed approach to the civilians on both sides, and we are going to show you something about what you call ethnic cleansing. What I would like to hear is whether it would have been useful. Would it have had an impact on your conclusions if you'd known what you know now? And another question: Do you know where the Serbs that had fled Gorazde ended up? Do you accept the fact that they were not far away, they were just on the other side of the confrontation line, in the very neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they had gone to, but I'll certainly take your word for it that they were close by, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if we go back to your propensity to use the term "siege," how would you reconcile that if you know that the Serbs from Gorazde fled only across the confrontation line? Is that also a siege or is it a defence of the Serbian villages around Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I used the word "siege" in relation to Gorazde because at the time that I went there in August of 1992, that was the word that was being used by the UNPROFOR and UNHCR people who were on the convoy, and they certainly -- I was reporting what they were doing, and they certainly regarded what they were doing was breaking a siege of Gorazde that had lasted since the start of the war. So that word was being used by the people putting together the convoy, and the intention -- their intention was to get in -- into that siege.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this clip, this video-clip, be admitted? 1D2925 is the number, Muslim attacks on the Serbian Army around Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D952, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Gorazde had not had the borders of the protected area determined, that there was no agreement to that effect, as there was for Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall whether or not a distinction was made in relation to safe areas, if that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to the international agreements and the Law of War, when a safe area is established, the warring parties have to agree to its borders and the applicable regime. The Muslim side was never in favour of doing that for Gorazde. They did it for Srebrenica and Zepa, but they never honoured that agreement, but, rather, launched attacks from the safe areas. Can we now see D950, page 2. It must not be broadcast, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was confirmed that it was a public document, wasn't it? We admitted it --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, thank you. I am overly cautious, even more than I need to be, it seems. D950, page 2, bullet point 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You reported about ethnic cleansing in Rogatica; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I did, I believe, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at bullet point 4 in that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to switch to e-court from Sanction. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please pay attention to bullet point 4. The general in question believes that that was part of the agreement between the two parties. Do you respect the opinions of the highly-positioned officials of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I respect his opinion, but the information that I had at the time, based on -- at the time, based on speaking to Muslims who were former residents of Rogatica, who got to Sarajevo, that they had an extremely hard time. There was talk of killing, there was talk of forcible evacuation, and there were also talks of -- talk of rapes. I spoke to young women who said they'd been raped at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you believe them; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported their allegations, certainly. I wasn't an eye-witness. They seemed like convincing witnesses to me, certainly in terms of long conversations I had with them, and the -- I think it would have been very hard for them to -- unless they were very, very accomplished actors, to act in the way that they did. And since they were 16-, 17-year-olds, I don't think they would have been capable of sustaining that level of deception. That was my opinion at the time, so we ran with the piece, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember allegations about 80.000 raped Muslim women, a crime which was ascribed to the Serbian state politics, and then it all boiled down to only 18 rape cases, which would have occurred over four years even in peacetime? Do you agree that the numbers, the figures, start at 80.000, and then at the end the number was reduced to a very small number, less than a thousand?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's over the top and inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Agreed. Move on to your next topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's go to ethnic cleansing, then. Yesterday, on page 20, between lines 13 and 16, you stated this -- this is yesterday's transcript: [In English] "What I meant was the expulsion, by force or by acts of terror, effectively parts of a population to render the community in which they had lived a place where there was only one -- one of the communities left. For example, Serbs kicked out Muslims. We saw there was a lot of that. Ethnic cleansing was a practice that all sides in the Bosnian war used, and all sides in the former Yugoslav wars, in fact, used it by -- but it was something that was really prevalent. It was one of the tenets of the war. You know, war is a question of -- I mean, how do you win wars? You win wars by inflicting damage on your enemy, by killing people, by destroying property, and also, in this particular case, by the shifting of population." [Interpretation] Let me not read on. I wouldn't agree -- or, rather, I hope, when you said "by killing people," you meant military personnel and not civilians; right? Can you just say yes or no? Did I understand you properly? You did not mean people, civilians; you meant troops, soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant what I said yesterday, elsewhere in my evidence, which was, sadly, the way that modern wars are fought, the preponderance of war, the overwhelming majority of casualties are civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then when you said "property," you probably didn't mean private property. You meant state property or the property of the opposing army; right? Not what actually happened, but what the intentions usually are, in terms of winning a war; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I meant all kinds of property. And I'm also aware, insofar as a journalist can be aware, of the various parts of international law that apply to bombardments and the concept of protected persons under that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you make a distinction between the shifting of a population and ethnic cleansing? In this particular paragraph or in yesterday's transcript, you mentioned the term "by the shift of population." Do you make a distinction between these two terms?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I came up with that form of words because you asked me to try to define it, or I was asked to try to define it. I'll repeat. My belief, based on what I saw and what I read about and research I did, was that all sides used ethnic cleansing, but the way it worked out, the Serb side used it most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. Do you know that when we signed -- when I say "signed," I mean the warring parties. We signed several agreements, sometimes under the auspices of the UNHCR, at other times under the auspices of Lord Carrington, Ambassador Cutileiro at the London Conference, subscribing to an obligation to provide the transport and escort to the civilian population who wished to be transferred from one area to another? The first such agreement was signed on the 22nd of May, 1992. That was repeated in June in London. In July 1992, that was during Carrington's conference, and then again in August, and it was repeated several times. The obligation of both sides was to allow the shifting of a population and to provide armed escorts in order to prevent people from being killed en route. Did you know about that? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember in detail the agreements that were signed at those particular conferences. I would have to look them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, Mr. Bowen, that "Jerusalem Post" published a fact that there were more Serb refugees than Muslim and Croat refugees together? Israel did not have any political interests in the Balkans. "The Jerusalem Post" published that, and that was not taken over by any of the Western media. Were you aware of the fact that this was published, that there were more Serb refugees than Muslim and Croat refugees together?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that "Jerusalem Post" report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Bowen, that in the Yugoslavian wars, the first mass exodus, and in autumn 1991 from Western Slavonia, and the last exodus in 1995 from Krajina involved the Serbs, and that in the meantime, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, almost all Serbs who could flee did flee the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Were you aware of all of that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of Western Slavonia. I was involved in the coverage of that part of that war. I'm also aware of what happened in Krajina. I travelled through Krajina in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that two-thirds of Sarajevan Serbs fled Sarajevo, and when the Dayton Accords were signed and when the embargo was lifted, almost all of them who had remained finally fled, and there is no more than 20.000 of them living in Sarajevo of the initial 120.000 who -- there's something wrong with the transcript. There are only about 20, and there were about 200 of them.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that after the -- I'm aware that -- yeah, I mean, I can't talk to you about the figures because I'm not aware of the figures, but I'm -- I have a fair understanding, I think, of the way that populations moved after the Dayton Accords were signed, and also the way that things are now, more or less, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serb side always provided buses and armed escorts, and the Muslim side never did that? When the Serbs wanted to flee, they had to rely on Croats, and they could carry nothing but plastic bags in their hands. Do you -- are you aware of the agreements signed on the auspices of the UNHCR and that the Serbs honoured those agreements, that they always provided buses and armed escorts for the Muslim civilians, whereas the Serbs, when they wanted to get out, they had to find their own means, they had to run across Croat territories?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a distinction needs to be made between ethnic cleansing at gunpoint, using fear and terror and killing people and the kind of things that I was reporting on in the early part of the war, and later organised movements of populations under the auspices of the UN. I think it's chalk and cheese, it's oranges and lemons, it's two different things there. I think one was possibly the consequence of the other. But I think in terms of the arrangements that were made as well, I can only comment on particular stories that I reported on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were in Mostar. You passed through Konjic and Jablanica. Do you know that 6.500 Serbs lived in Konjic, and in Mostar and in the Neretva Valley, 44.000 Serb lived, and do you know what happened to them, what was their lot? Yes or no. Just a simple answer, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the numbers. I knew there was Serbs there, and I knew as well that there was ethnic cleansing in those parts of the -- as I said, all sides did it at different times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Defence puts it to you, Mr. Bowen, that the Serbs honoured the obligation on the temporary shift of the population and that the Serbs were chased from the Federation of Bosnia and -- from the Bosnian Federation, and they were killed there, with some honourable exceptions when Croats helped up. Mr. Bowen, did you find a single Serbian village in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina that remained intact? Could you give us a name of a single Serb village in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was not destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there before the war, so I don't quite know what the status quo before the war was, in terms of who lived where. The kinds of things I was reporting on were the movements that were happening while I was there; for example, those people who were coming into Travnik. I mean, as a reporter, I can only report what I see when I'm there, of course trying to under the wider context. But I think I've already answered your questions on the relative amounts of ethnic cleansing that were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are trying to establish the numbers. Do you know that there were municipalities in Republika Srpska where no Muslim person was touched? Do you know that there were many villages or small townships, like Janja, where Muslims could live, and many of them remained living there until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I wasn't aware of that. As I say, I reported on those incidents of ethnic cleansing that occurred while I was in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, in your report, 65 ter 4049E, we hear you say that a refugee told you that they had had to bribe a Serb soldier in Bosanski Petrovac in order to be able to leave. Remind me, what did they pay for? Did they pay the Serb soldier to allow them to stay or to allow them to leave? Maybe we should watch the video-clip again to jog your memory.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. I mean, let's watch it. I don't think we talked about exactly what the price was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're not talking about the actual price, but the purpose. What did they pay for? Did they pay to be able to stay in Petrovac or to be able to leave Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the meaning of the report was that they were paying to leave that town unmolested and unharmed. Well, unharmed, not unmolested. The refugees in that refugee centre in Travnik came out with overwhelming amounts of testimony to the way that they were treated badly by Serb forces, and as you'll recall, there was talk of it being a reprisal for the deaths of some Serb fighters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to play that clip?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can play the clip, although the witness has already confirmed that they paid to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How can you reconcile that with the claim that they were chased away at a gunpoint?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because that's what the vast majority said. I said that this one particular individual then had to pay a bribe presumably to leave without being further harmed. But as you'll recall from that report, sir, there was a lot of testimony about people witnessing the killings of members of their families in front of them. There was a woman, for example, talking about her daughter being shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, do you know that there is no single place in Republika Srpska without Muslims or Croats who remained living there throughout the war? Do you know that there was not a single ethnically uniform place in Republika Srpska, despite the fact that many had left for various reasons? Do you know that there was no single ethnically-uniform area in Republika Srpska that had been populated with a mixed population before the war?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really comment on those statements that you make about the spread of population. What I knew about Bosnia-Herzegovina was that the populations were, to a greater or lesser extent, relatively mixed before the war and that what we've seen during and since is that now there are blocks of population as a result of ethnic cleansing and subsequent movements of the population after the war, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, as a journalist, did you investigate the difference between Muslims and Croats who remained living in Republika Srpska peacefully throughout the war, they held their jobs, they participated in the police and the army, and those Muslims and Croats who decided to ask the municipalities to allow them to leave or to leave of their own will? Did you investigate that as a journalist? How come that some Croats and Muslims decided to stay, as opposed to the others, who decided to leave? What was the difference between the two groups?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe there were some Muslims and Croats in the Bosnian Serb Army, but I never met them. What I do remember are things like the long -- the large, expansive, empty villages. Once you went through Brcko and went west through Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was almost nothing. There were fields that were absolutely uncultivated, homes that had been -- the roofs gone, the window frames gone and burnt out, villages abandoned, and an absence of people who had been living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there a single Muslim village that you came across there? Who lived in these villages?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who -- no one was living in them as we drove past. I don't recall, in that area, going through a single Muslim-populated village, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, those were Christian villages, sir. There was not a single Muslim village there, but we'll get to that. 1D2941, can we have that in e-court now. Let us see what a Croat, a Catholic, a much better Catholic than you are, says about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time. It's time to take a break. And I note that you've had, so far, four hours and 15 minutes, which means you will have 45 minutes to conclude your cross-examination during the next session. I have one thing to deal with briefly in the absence of the witness, so we will allow the witness to be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1.00, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we go into --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say something in relation to this? Can I ask for another 45 minutes, because we need to deal, in very specific terms, with a great many statements made in such an arbitrary fashion by this witness. We cannot disregard the fact that he made so many cavalier statements, and we need to know what he meant by them. I'm not asking for much. I'm asking for 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You could have been more efficient so far, but I will consult my colleagues. How much would you expect for your re-examination, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Presently, something in the neighbourhood of 10 minutes or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you will have another -- an additional half an hour, which means that we cannot go to the next witness today. Given the time, we'll begin the next session in the absence of the witness to deal with a matter. 12.00. I'm sorry, 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's related to the motion to subpoena Mr. Zecevic, Mr. Tieger. I noted Mr. Robinson's statement that he's opposed to the subpoena, Zecevic being an expert witness. And at one point in time, the Prosecution indicated it would be offering his evidence as expert witness -- as expert evidence, but in the monthly witness list, nor in the motion itself, there's no reference to Rule 94 bis for this witness. So I wonder whether Mr. Zecevic is being called as an expert, or a factual witness, or both. So whether you can clarify this. This may assist the Defence and the Chamber in resolving the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I think the latter characterisation is accurate in that sense. I'd like to check with Mr. Gaynor to see if my current understanding of the proposed testimony is accurate. However, I think for purposes of this motion, I think the Court has a generally accurate understanding of that, and I am -- and I think what the Court wants to know, in particular, is whether there will be a specific submission pursuant to 94 bis, and I'll get the response to the Court by the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you will have up to quarter past 2.00. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just so I'm not thought poorly of, I've upped my estimate by five minutes, if I may, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you'll have 15 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem. Thank you, Mr. Bowen. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I please have 1D24 -- actually, 2941. You talked about Banja Luka and these towns, and now let us hear what a good Catholic and a good Croat, at that, says about the status of Croats in Banja Luka in October 1993. 1D2941. There is even a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's switch to e-court. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please see the translation as well. Could we have the Serbian version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is the 4th of October, 1993. Jadranko Prlic, as prime minister of Herceg-Bosna, visited Banja Luka, and this is what he says: "My wish to visit Banja Luka and to convince myself that Croatian people live here was realised today, because political conditions in that regard have been established. Serbs and Croats in these areas did not wage war. The majority of Croats remained in Banja Luka, which is a result of the positive attitude of Republika Srpska. Therefore, the departure of Croats from these areas should be prevented, their moving out of apartments, that should be regulated by law ..." This is what Jadranko Prlic said, and now he is referring to economic co-operation as well because he is prime minister, after all. Do you know that most Croats in Banja Luka stayed on throughout in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference I made to Croats was simply something about that church that I visited that was shut up and covered in graffiti. My impression in Banja Luka was that the population that suffered there most was the Muslim population because of the -- you could -- it was documented that a substantial number of mosques were demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know about this visit on the 4th of October, 1993? A year and a half after the war started, Jadranko Prlic visited Banja Luka and established economic co-operation. Had you known that at the time and had you known how many Croats had stayed on in Banja Luka, would that have meant something to you? I do, though, accept the criticism voiced that we were not good enough at informing the general public.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only time I met Mr. Prlic was in this courtroom, when I testified in his case. I wasn't aware of that visit, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You know the position of the Chamber. A third person's statement is not admitted unless the maker of the statement confirms the veracity of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a piece of news from the newspapers, from the media in "Srpski Glas" of the 4th. Perhaps I omitted to mention that "Glas Srpski" is a daily newspaper that carried this particular piece of news. So if that changes things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All the more so with the media article. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know, Mr. Bowen, that some municipalities had asked for many documents from Muslims who wanted to leave the municipality concerned? Banja Luka, as the most liberal, asked for only 15 documents to be compiled, such as certificates, that tax had been paid, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the exact bureaucratic procedure. I did report in that piece from Travnik that they had been forced to sign over some property. There was a document which one of the refugees was brandishing with an official stamp on it that was in the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did that spur this kind of thing? Did people prefer leaving rather than staying? If people are asking you for lots of documents, does it make it easier for you to stay or to leave?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. The people I spoke to uniformly said that they were -- had been terrorised and forced from their homes, and they spoke also of people being beaten and shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why, then, Mr. Bowen, would they be asked to collect documents, and they would spend a month collecting all of these documents in order to be able to leave? Why would that happen if they were being expelled from their homes? The two are incompatible, Mr. Bowen. I'm not talking about individuals here. I'm talking about the behaviour of state organs. Do you know that state organs made it more difficult for Croats and Muslims to leave or to move out of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm or deny that assertion that you've just made. I did note, in my reporting and in my evidence, that I -- that the nature of ethnic cleansing changed as the war went on, from people arriving in the middle of the night with guns, at the beginning, to that more bureaucratic process that we saw, that we reported on in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Bowen, that we needed some time to establish a state based on the rule of law, and that we did not have one in April, May, June and July, perhaps not even in September 1992? Our state was a Greenfield project, so time was required to establish a state based on the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree or disagree with that, Dr. Karadzic. I'm not able to comment on the condition of the administration that you had at that particular time. I think that's a question for you, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that none of these certificates that were required by municipalities -- actually, these requests to have property signed away, do you know that I annulled that already in August 1992? None of this was actually carried through.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that piece was July or August 1992 in Travnik. I wasn't aware of that edict that you issued. No, I'm sorry, I beg your pardon. For the record, it was September or October that piece was broadcast, that Travnik piece, of 1992. It wasn't the summer; it was early autumn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But these refugees spoke about what had happened before August; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were speaking about what had happened in the last couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you did not know that I had annulled that by this decision with the force of law; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about your -- no, that piece of -- that order that you sent out, no, I didn't know that. But it sounds as though neither did the people in Prijedor or in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, they didn't know during the first two months because communications were down, but they did find out, and all of it was annulled. Do you accept that, that it was annulled and that it was not carried through anywhere?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't accept that, because the first I've heard of your annulment of that is in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When speaking about Gorazde - let us go back to that briefly - you confirmed that Serbs were furious because the Muslims had used the convoy as a human shield and attacked Serb positions, killing eight soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was their belief. We were taken to see the bodies of the soldiers who were recently killed. You could tell from the condition of the corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know of our official position, that after every convoy, Muslim attacks against us were intensified, and that all of that made us suspect that convoys were delivering ammunition and weaponry to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know of that official position, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now link this up with Cerska. Do you know that we sent a message to Cerska, and all these other villages there, that they should not fight because their villages would probably belong to the Muslim constituent unit?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that message.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that for an entire year, from the spring of 1992 until the spring of 1993, they shot our troops in the back, they ambushed civilians, they killed civilians on buses, they would kill an entire busload of people or a car full of people? Do you know that they harassed us all the time and that we sustained heavy losses?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there was fighting around the fringes of the enclave, but I didn't have the details of what was happening, in terms of -- with that kind of precision that you have just alleged, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am dealing with what you had said; namely, that a convoy to Cerska had been agreed upon, but was then stopped in Zvornik, and that afterwards you were informed that Serbs had taken Cerska. Do you know that Muslims, just like in Gorazde, abused the arrival of the convoy near Cerska, and that that is why you had been stopped?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one mentioned that to me at the time. No, I didn't know that. We were still some way from Cerska, and we -- while we were stopped there, we had -- the convoy people, I should say, had quite a lot of messages from the Serb side saying that, Yes, shortly it will all happen, you will go forward. There was sort of reassurance that was being put around, which is why they waited there, I think, some period of several days, because they were hoping that the problems could be sorted out. But no one spoke to me of the sort of events that you describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that a large-scale media campaign was launched to the effect that we had carried out a terrible massacre of civilians in Cerska, and that that went on until General Morillon entered Cerska with media crews? Do you remember that campaign regarding Cerska that is identical to the media campaign involving Srebrenica in 1995? All the media were saying that we had massacred the population of Cerska?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember those allegations about Cerska. I do remember the Srebrenica events, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to Srebrenica. Thank you. Do you accept that in that zone, after Cerska and Kamenica were liberated, over 50 mass graves were found, containing 5 to 50 corpses of Serbs, and that General Morillon attended the burials?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken to the unearthing of what a Serb officer said was a mass grave of Serbs who were massacred. That was his allegation. I wasn't able to -- I think, from memory, I'm pretty sure they were uniformed corpses that were being disinterred. The UN and the military people who were with us - we were with the French Foreign Legion - suggested there was also a possibility that they may have been killed in the general fighting that was going on there, but I have no idea about the circumstances -- the precise circumstances of their deaths, no. But I saw one mass grave, I think, with around eight, ten bodies, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many Serb prisoners, that had been taken by the Muslims over that year in Cerska, were returned to us?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would it help you if I said not a single one? They had all been killed, massacred. If they had -- even if they were wearing uniforms, they should not have been killed or massacred; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, prisoners shouldn't be killed or massacred. But I have no idea what happened to prisoners in Cerska, because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you were not in very many places, Mr. Bowen, and you are testifying as if you had been there. Cerska, Bratunac, and in other areas, do you agree that over 3.200 civilians were killed, or, rather, Serbs, most of them civilians? We have the names and surnames, and we're going to provide the Trial Chamber with these names and surnames. However, do you accept that, that before 1995, over 3.200 Serbs had been killed there?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't accept that. I'm not familiar with the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bowen, accuracy and impartiality is the bible of the BBC, which merits our respect, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness has said he doesn't know the figure. There's no point of continuing that line of questions. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us now have a look at Srebrenica. In paragraph 68, you said that you were in Sarajevo when Srebrenica fell to the Bosnian-Serbian advance in 1995. You monitored Pale TV, and so on and so forth. That's was say. And then you say: [In English] "a few days later, the ICRC evacuated the women and children. I did daily report about what was going on, as far as it was possible to tell from Sarajevo at that time. The very first thing I noticed about the picture from Srebrenica was that there were no men to be seen. I guessed that they had been taken off to be detained and perhaps killed. In my report for the BBC, I mentioned that there were no men in the pictures." [Interpretation] First of all, do you accept that, that civilians from Srebrenica were evacuated to Potocari by the UN, that they were not expelled by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I say in the statement ICRC, maybe it was the UN, were -- yeah, I think they were there, and they were operating for some of the women and children. We also -- which I didn't say in the statement, but was in the report that was put in yesterday as evidence. We filmed quite large numbers of civilians, women and children in the main, walking in into Tuzla, who had crossed on foot, in no kind of organised way, from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You claim that the refugees walked from Srebrenica to Tuzla, that they fled on foot; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what they were telling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you that from their houses to Potocari, the refugees went on their own initiative, and then from Potocari to Kladanj, by various means of transport, and that some other people walked from Srebrenica to Tuzla. How come it never occurred to you that there may have been something else going on involving Muslims? Why it never occurred to you that they decided to attempt an armed breakthrough towards Tuzla? Do you know that there was a column of 15.000 men trying to breakthrough to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard different kinds of stories about that particular time, and I'm not qualified to judge what's true and what isn't, in terms of those precise circumstances of people who were trying to get out of Srebrenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bowen, one would expect that from you. You offer a lot of statements that the Defence cannot accept, that the Defence challenges, but those are notorious facts. 15.000 men actually attempted a breakthrough with arms, and they were on foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are, Mr. Karadzic, very argumentative with this witness. Just ask questions. The witness already said he doesn't know that story.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In my opinion, he should know, as an investigating journalist who reported from the area. That is my chief objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, you said on page 65 yesterday - it is in yesterday's transcript and you quoted from one of your reports - that I was talking about the superiority of the Serbian people on Pale Television. Do you know that I also consider Muslims ethnic Serbs and that under no condition would I ever think, let alone say, that one people is superior to the other? Can you confirm what is it that I actually said? Did I use the term "a superior people" or "a superior military force"?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given the translation at the time. As I've said, I can't speak Serbian. I do remember you telling me in interviews, I think, during the war period that your belief was that Muslims started out as Serbs and converted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, when they converted, they did not change their ethnic background. However, in the original language, I said "the superiority of the Serbian arms." Can you accept that there is a difference between the superiority of a people and the superiority of one's arms, and can you accept it when I say that I would never issue such a racist statement ever?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it was mistranslated, it was mistranslated. Unfortunately, I had to rely on the services of someone who was translating the language for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I can only regret that you didn't double-check, like you didn't double-check many other things, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can answer that. I do double-check a lot of things, and I often go very assiduously through translations with translators. But, I mean, I think the Serbian is on the tape, so no doubt those in the court who speak the language will be able to examine it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 69, you say: [In English] "It was known that the enclave of Eastern BiH were organised and had weapons and they were fighting. Otherwise, they would have been wrapped up by the Bosnian Serbs. It seemed credible and obvious to me that BiH government forces would fight. They were surrounded and had every reason to suppose they were fighting for their lives." [Interpretation] Mr. Bowen, you were the only well-informed person who could have claimed that. Do you know that those enclaves were supposed to be demilitarised and that the Secretary-General of the UN stated they were not demilitarised, but they were, rather, strongholds of the Muslim Army?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they clearly weren't demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that when one zone is proclaimed a safe area, with the consent of the warring parties, then that area cannot be armed, and also that no attacks are supposed to be launched from inside of those areas, nor can the other side attack anybody inside those areas?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that the safe area policy had rules, but the facts were that attacks were going back and forth and that there was fighting going on. That was well documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a single Serb attack that was not a counter-offensive, any Serb movement that did not constitute a counter-offensive?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on all sides of every part of the Balkan wars that I covered, from Croatia in 1991 to Kosovo in 1999, nobody said they shot first. Everybody said they were fighting back. That's a refrain I heard many, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, it is well known what Naser Oric's unit did to the neighbouring Serb villages. Let's go back to the issue of siege. Is it a siege if the Serbs around Srebrenica protected their own villages, if those villages suffered attacks day and night, the attacks coming from the so-called protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the military tactic used, as I understood it, by the Serb forces around Srebrenica was effectively to besiege the enclave. The enclave established a perimeter which they defended, and as I understand it, it was -- I've actually never been to Srebrenica, but it was an extended rural area with a number of settlements, and that things went back and forth. The exact day to day of the -- of the fighting there, I don't have a record of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I put it to you that they extended those safe areas by means of arms, illegally and in contravention of the agreement, that they killed the Serbs, that they virtually connected Srebrenica and Zepa by constantly exposing the Serb villages to attacks, does this sound plausible to you?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's one view of what was going on there. I've heard other views of what was going on there. And it's one view, also, of what was going on there at a particular time. Military fortunes rose and fell, I think, in the course of the war in that particular part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 69, you say: [In English] "It was clear, though, that their isolation and limitations on resupply meant that their combat effectiveness was going to be limited." Mr. Bowen, precisely because of that, we inspected the convoys. That is why we imposed restrictions, because they resupplied themselves with ammunition across our territory. It was our right, according to international laws, to control and to prescribe conditions under which they would be resupplied and receive aid. The restrictions were imposed on limiting their combat capabilities, and I believe that that was our legitimate right, to do that.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear what your question is, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. I think the witness has answered in any event. I think you are approaching the time to conclude your cross-examination. No, he has time, but given the quality of questions. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, you were familiar with the situation in Sarajevo, to a certain extent. You were not familiar with every position. Were you familiar with the so-called generals of the Muslim Army, Caco, Juka, Celo, who commanded brigades in that town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of their names, and they were figures at the time of, for some people, great notoriety. For other people, they were figures who were much to be admired. They were certainly controversial figures, those three that you mentioned, so I was aware of those names, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that they were removed at the moment when they turned their arms against their own police, they killed or murdered the son of the police minister, and threatened to take over the command of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was best aware of Caco and his operations, because I knew someone who was in one of his units. And, no, I was aware that he was a very controversial figure and that, in the end, the government forces turned against him and there was -- and they removed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they turned against him? Do you know that Caco and his unit killed a huge number of Serbs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of some of their activities. It was quite hard to report on them, because they were very hostile to journalists. The one time I managed to get into his part of town that he controlled, I certainly saw them taking parties of people they regarded as slackers, who weren't taking part in the war effort, I saw them being pushed up to the front-line at gunpoint, presume -- carrying shovels, so presumably to dig trenches. And he was someone who started off with a good reputation, as a kind of Robin Hood, because he broke open food warehouses and gave food to some of the population, and then later on he had -- among quite large numbers of people in Sarajevo, he had a bad reputation because of the undisciplined and violent behaviour of some of his own men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You certainly do not dispute the fact that he was the one who killed the son of the minister of the police, and that it was only then when the government finally turned against him? Before that, he didn't have any problems. While he was killing all the Serbs, nothing happened to him.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite remember who it was that -- I do remember that he killed someone that was prominent. I don't remember who, exactly, or that his people did. I'm not -- the facts of that -- particular precise facts of that case, I'm not -- it's probably better if I don't try and speculate about them. But I do know that they did turn against him and that his power then ended.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 1D2917. This is a part of your book. Can it be displayed in e-court, 1D2917. Can we see page 141 in the book, not in e-court. 141 in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that he was executed --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it on there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is a part of your statement. I am looking for your book, which is 1D2917 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is D936.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree and do you remember that he was executed only in the autumn of 1993, in October or November 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date of his execution. I'm not sure if I knew it, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've been listening to this for a long time, and I'm more convinced now than ever that this is -- this line of questioning and this evidence is tu quoque, and I would be objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to respond, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do -- I intend to show what the attitude of the Serb side was towards Sarajevo, as opposed to the attitude of the Muslim side towards Sarajevo. This man was a general, Juka Prazina was a general, Caco was a general, and they were notorious criminals who killed the Serbs first. And then when there were no longer any Serbs to kill, they turned against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the paragraph which starts with the words: "The Bosnian government ...," which is the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wait, Mr. Karadzic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, perhaps you can assist. This line of cross-examination dealing with these individuals, is this something of which you have an intimate knowledge or are you simply relying upon, as it were, the general information which you had at the time that would have been available to anybody making a reasoned inquiry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a little bit of information which is in the book from one of the people who fought with Caco, which I put down. I never met the guy, himself. It also says "Celo." There was more than one Celo. The one I met was someone who, in the first part of the war, was seen locally as a military hero, and then as I say in the book, a year or so later, by that stage, he had moved into a wider range of activities and then he was behaving like a gangster. But that's about what I know. I certainly didn't have intimate dealings with him, and in no sense would I -- I'm basing what I know is down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, if that's the case, then really you may find it's much more useful, bearing in mind the limited time that you have, to move on from this particular topic, because there's an obvious way that you can get any of evidence related to these matters before the Court, other than through a witness who's indicated the limitations of his information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will abandon the topic, although the witness did write about it in this book. And in this paragraph, you can see a reference to this being a private army, and so on and so forth. In the same document, can we look at page 151. I'm moving on to an entirely different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, you told us, and I know that for a fact, that the BBC bible pinpoints at accuracy and impartiality; right?
