utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Accuracy and impartiality are very important, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the first paragraph on page 151. You will see that you stated your political views, and you sided against the Serbs here; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What it says is: "We should have been harder on the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs, who were treated by Western governments and their ..." Well, you can read it: "... as legitimate people with whom business could be done." I think what I'm saying there is my reporting was impartial, but it might have been a bit more accurate had we been a little harder on those activities that were taking place that we saw. In the quest -- what I think I was trying to say was in the quest for impartiality, we moved possibly a little bit away from accuracy by not stating definitively enough the kind of things that were being done in the name of the -- in this case, the Serb people. There's a balance to be drawn. In impartial reporting, there's a balance to be drawn between stating things that are true and stating the wider context, and it's always a fine judgement to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bowen, I'm questioning your -- the appropriateness of your testimony against me. You say here the indictments, in themselves, are proof that they are responsible. In other words, you see indictments as convictions. I'm trying to see whether your political engagement and your political position against the Serbs and against the Croats, as was seen in Judge Antonetti's trial, and Judge Antonetti had serious objections against your views, would that disqualify you as a witness? Is it a fact that you stated here that an indictment is a good-enough proof of somebody's responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd agree that that sentence isn't well written. I should have put "allegedly" in there. It's clear that an indictment is not a conviction. I think perhaps I was trying to refer to the respective volumes of indictments that were -- that had -- at the time of writing, had been handed down. But I agree that I could have drafted that sentence more precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page or, rather, this paragraph be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be add to the existing Exhibit D936.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The following page, please: [In English] "Most Serbs were descent, hospitable people, and I often felt sorry for them. They were led into a catastrophe by Slobodan Milosevic, Radovan Karadzic, and the rest, who ..." [Interpretation] Next page, please. 154, at the very top: [In English] "... Radovan Karadzic, and the rest, who manipulated their historic insecurity and used nationalism ruthlessly and cynically to secure their own power." [Interpretation] You think and you say in your book that I did all that in order to secure my power. Do you know that in 1990, I did not put up my candidacy anywhere, that I did not want to be in power?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you were doing in 1990, but I know that in the time that I was reporting on what was going on, you were the leader. And it was clear that nationalism, in the whole of the former Yugoslavia, was being used and abused, and I think it's -- I would -- I said that earlier sentence was not well written. I think that sentence is absolutely true. I think that historic insecurities were manipulated and nationalism was used ruthlessly as a vehicle to gain and to keep power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, do you know that Muslims had planned and informed, accordingly, their Western allies, particularly Croats and, through them, also Americans, that they had planned to throw out all Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just said that I think all sides used nationalism. A major cause of the wars of Yugoslavia was that heady and dangerous atmosphere of nationalism and the abuse of those concepts and people's fears by all leaders. Izetbegovic and Tudjman were also, I would say, responsible and guilty for that kind of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I heard that you would say that in the second edition of your book, because the first edition doesn't contain that. The only ones that you accuse here are the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page be added -- or, rather, the two pages that we've just seen, can they be added? And then can we also look at page 169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 169, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at your political views, which cast doubt on your appropriateness as a witness? Look here. You did not trust even your own government, in other words? You doubt the motives of the British government: [In English] "I thought there was one easy way to end the misery and suffering in Sarajevo, and that was to break the siege by attacking the Bosnian Serbs on their hills. But the government of John Major was urging caution, not action." [Interpretation] And a bit further down: [In English] "Douglas Hurd, the former secretary, dismissed journalists like me as the 'something must be done' club." [Interpretation] Now, you think that the Serb villages around Sarajevo and the Serb suburbs should have been bombed and handed over to the Muslims, while expelling the Serbs. Your government was cautious, and you were objecting to that. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're misinterpreting my words and you're taking them out of context. I didn't say that. The point I'm making there is that, yeah, of course I have beliefs of my own, but I'm saying I didn't put them in my reporting. And that, I hope, is clear from the videos that have been submitted. In the end, I'm right in saying that that was effectively what happened in 1995. They decided to go ahead, and there were air-strikes, and the stalemate ended. I did have suspicions about the political motives of the British Government at the time, yes, and as a journalist, I have to tell you I'm paid to have suspicions about people's motives. That's what we do. So just because people say that it's true doesn't mean that it is. In that particular case, if you read all the paragraphs around it and the pages around it, what I'm specifically referring to was medical evacuation. I felt that the British Government seized on some highly publicised cases in 1993, particularly the case of Irma Hadzimuratovic, but others as well, and expedited the evacuations, and I thought quite a cynical way, because at the time there was a lot of pressure in the newspapers for action, and the newspapers I had -- not the BBC -- for action to end the suffering of people in Sarajevo, and I think that the British Government found that was a way of giving an impression of moving without doing a great deal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page be admitted, or, rather, can be added to the same number, 169?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you would have resolved that faster. Would it have been simpler to alleviate the suffering of Sarajevo by handing it over to the UN, as the Serbs had proposed, themselves, or was it better to bomb the Serbs and let the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina prevail? Do you know that that is what our offer had been, to hand over Sarajevo to the UN?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that offer. In 1995, there were air-strikes against Serb positions, and that was followed by the political process that led to the Dayton Agreements. I think what I'm saying here is they could have done that a year or two earlier, had they so wished, and that would have saved quite a few lives. I'm certainly not suggesting, in that paragraph or at any time, that what they should have done, as I think you suggested a little while ago, was to used military force to hand the place over to the Muslim government. That was not my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, Mr. Bowen, that these stances are preeminently political and that this is political activism? It's not exactly neutral. On the contrary, it is decidedly anti-Serb.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That book was written 10 years after the events which we're describing. What I'm saying, in a few lines there, is that I didn't report my own beliefs, I didn't report my own beliefs. I reported what was happening as a journalist. But, you know, I'm a thinking person, so clearly I have a mind of my own about things, but I'm not a political activity. And I think to suggest that those few lines are political activism is, frankly, a gross exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought that I did not have to resort to this, but now let us actually see what your position is, as a whole, with regard to the parties. Can I have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2915.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the text? You must have read it in April 2009. It has to do with your violation of instructions on accuracy in your reporting from Israel.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Explaining the context of this, I'm afraid, is not an easy thing to do and it might take a while, but I'm very glad to. And now that you've raised this, I think I should. In my position -- my current position which I've had since 2005 as the BBC's Middle East editor, I'm suggest to a large number of criticisms, complaints, formal and informal, by people who are party to their conflict going on in the Middle East and who are supporters of the different sides there. There's a constant process of complaining going on, and the BBC has quite a complex complaints procedure which I won't bore you with the details of. But suffice it to say, the highest level of it is the BBC Trust. In the course of one of their adjudications, on which they cleared me of a large number of things, they found me as it says there. They ruled on complaints that -- on two small points. Now, that was a very controversial ruling. I'm not going to repeat conversations I had with members of the trust afterwards, but I will say things that the BBC management, itself, said to me. My immediate bosses in the BBC expressed full confidence in my reporting. There was no official censure from them. There's no censure at all. What I had, in fact, was, in private, continuous expressions of support for my reporting. And the point also has to be made that these complaints were made by professional lobbyists, in one case a paid lobbyist from a particularly aggressive right-wing organisation in the United States, not a BBC license pair, and they persuaded, essentially, a lay panel to rule on some issues in the Middle East. And there were elements of the ruling which were nonsensical. One thing which I need to mention -- I'm aware of the pressure of time here, so I'll try and keep it brief. They said, for example, that that -- one of the statements I made was inaccurate because I didn't give -- I didn't -- I didn't name my source. Had I named my source, the statement would have become accurate. That's clearly a nonsense. It was a flawed ruling by the BBC Trust. I have reason to believe that members of that -- that there is some regret about that. There was a widespread opposition to it, and I think that -- I certainly don't accept -- I have to accept their ruling. I don't believe that it's true. So the context of that, certainly there were these findings against me, but the -- I think the key point is that I'm still employed as the BBC Middle East editor, I still report the way that I've always reported, and that I've been given, privately and publicly, the full confidence of my employers. So that, I hope, gives some context to that particular ruling by the BBC Trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often does that happen? How often does the BBC make this kind of ruling, censuring its editor, in a way? When did that last happen?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness said he did not -- he was not censured in any way whatsoever, in fact. That's a misstatement of what Mr. Bowen has just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you reprimanded? Were you censured in any way?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the trust state something?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the trust stated what you've got there in that report of it, though I suggest that you would be better served if you looked at their full report, because it goes at great length -- at great length, it describes how it rejects many of the complaints against me. But that particular -- there are two small points that they found on, and that's -- that was the end of it. There was pointedly -- pointedly, from the management of the BBC News, there was no censuring of me, there was no disciplinary action. There were expressions of support, which some of the -- they were more pointed, I have to say, in private than in public because of the relative positions of the BBC and the BBC Trust and the way that it works. The BBC Trust is the regulator of the BBC, but it is also, in a sense, of the BBC, so its discussions in public are difficult. But I certainly have no reason to doubt that I have the full confidence of the BBC management, that by -- 26 years with the BBC count as a great deal of experience, and I have, therefore, their full confidence as the BBC Middle East editor. And if I didn't have that confidence, I wouldn't be doing the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bowen. Mr. Karadzic, you'll have three minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at another document. That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D -- what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D953, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, while we're waiting for this, I'm a bit worried. You do not accept the views of high-ranking, highly-educated UN officers. You criticise your own government because of its attitude towards the Serbs. And now you don't seem to like the BBC Trust either. Is this heading not sufficient: "Jeremy Bowen breached the guide-lines --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on. Mr. Karadzic, move on to your next topic. Where is the next document? The last, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2932, can we have that displayed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the nature of the civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina here. I cannot really find my way here.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at the document about the Middle East complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The video. We no longer have enough time to deal with this. However, the first one, the BBC Trust -- or, rather, the finding was that you had breached instructions. Now let us view the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That was not the finding. The witness has just explained that, Your Honours. It's another misstatement of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: In fact, in the document, it will say that the Har Homa -- that Mr. Bowen's Har Homa report was cleared by the trust over issues of impartiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's play the video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then have the previous one -- or, actually, after the video, we are going to show that front page, where it says that he did, indeed, violate it. It's a different matter, whether they're going to punish him or not. However, the ruling of the trust has to do with two issues, two minor issues, as Bowen says. But, nevertheless, that is what the ruling states, that it is a violation of the impartiality principle. But let's have the video first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: When I first came to cover the war in what we now call the former Yugoslavia, about a year ago, when it was all starting, people used to talk about the atrocities perpetrated against their grandparents in the Second World War or even further back during the time of the Ottoman Empire, for instance. The difference now is that people talk about the atrocity perpetrated last week. The sad thing is that a new generation of people have learned how to hate and they've learned how to kill, sometimes killing the people they used to play with as children. As a journalist, the longer you spend here, the more pessimistic you get. I think all of us covering the war in Sarajevo believe that it's all going to get much worse and there's nothing the world can do about it."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Bowen, this clip shows that you are fully aware of the profound historical and social conditionality of that war. And in the book you accuse me and Milosevic, saying that it is a result of what we wanted. Do you stand by what you said in this video-clip?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do stand by what I said in that video-clip from 1992. But what I'd also say was in the book, I was referring to the manipulation of their historical insecurities of the Serb people. History plays a big part in people's view of the world very often, even if they don't quite realise that, and the point I was making was that the media and nationalistically-minded leaders manipulated the histories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did Milosevic and Karadzic carry out manipulations from 1941 until 1945, when 700.000 Serbs were killed, 100.000 Jews, and so on? Were we the ones who were doing the manipulating then or is what you say in this video-clip true?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you don't have to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Isn't the point, Dr. Karadzic, that that's exactly what Mr. Bowen is saying, is that history is replete with examples, and he's simply giving his view? Whether or not it's an accurate view is a matter for decision, but the view is that we are governed as we are, are we not, by history and our view of history? Isn't that something which is just simply part of the human condition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Karadzic, as for the BBC Trust's ruling, I think we have heard enough. Unless you have a final question, I will give the floor to Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at the second paragraph here: [In English] "The second complaint --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I said we've heard enough, unless you have another question on a separate topic for your final question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'd like to ask Mr. Bowen whether -- actually, I'm always scared and cautious when Serbs and Jews do not fare well, then a world war is imminent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know something we don't know? Is there going to be a Third World War, Mr. Bowen?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit the last clip as Exhibit D954. And Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I can't see my way any shorter than holding to my 15 minutes, just so you're aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, earlier today Dr. Karadzic asked you, at pages 81 to 84 of this transcript, a number of questions about the -- about Cerska, which you wrote about and tried to travel to and the events there. Among them, he noted there his official position that after every convoy, Muslim attacks against us were intensified, and that made them suspect that convoys were delivering ammunition. He asked you about sending a message to Cerska and other villages that they shouldn't fight because their villages would probably belong to a Muslim constituent unit. Do you remember that line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a couple of documents relating to Cerska, the first being 65 ter 3979. And that, Mr. Bowen, is a document from the Drina Corps Command of the Bosnian Serb Army, dated 24 November - pardon me - 1992 to the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade Command. Please let me know when you see the English version on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I've got it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Bowen, this document reads, in the first paragraph: "Pursuant to the directive of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska strictly confidential number 2/5 of 19 November 1992 and an assessment of the situation, I have decided: "Launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up, or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the areas of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde." And I've just read you paragraph 1. Now, if we could go over on to the next page, bottom of the next page in English, paragraph 2.3(c), do you see it on the very bottom of the screen?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this paragraph talks about moral and psychological preparations, saying: "Before initiating any kind of operation, inform the unit members about the important aim of that operation and underline that the outcome of minor actions and of the whole operation is of a crucial importance for the realisation of the aim of the Serbian people; namely, the creation and establishment of a Serbian state in those areas." And it's signed and stamped by Commander Colonel Milenko Zivanovic. Now, what I'd like to ask you is whether you see any relationship between this document, given its date, and the events you reported on when you attempted to enter Cerska while it was being taken in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just remind me of the date of the document? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 24 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's -- it clarifies a lot of things for me. Clearly, we weren't privy to these kinds of documents at the time, but it bears out the sorts of things which I think that we were reporting; that there was a military project to create that Serb state.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have that document, please, marked as a Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2085, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I next have 65 ter 1209.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bowen, this is a document dated 3 March 1993, from Mrs. Sadako Ogata, from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, to Dr. Karadzic. Now, can you see the first paragraph of this document?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That states: "The reports I receive on the situation in Cerska are appalling. A large number of civilians are blocked in areas which are under military attack. The number of casualties is reportedly high. It is, therefore, imperative that immediate relief be brought to the victims." Now, Mr. Bowen, do you have any comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was about the time that I was with the UNHCR convoy protected by the French Foreign Legion, trying to get into Cerska, and stopped on the road. I think we -- probably a little bit before that document was written. So, yes, we were with quite a large convoy of relief supplies which were blocked and eventually turned back, and we subsequently learned that at the time we were being turned back was the time that Cerska was falling.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would this be marked, please, as a Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2086, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at page 71 of today's transcript, lines 4 to 6, Dr. Karadzic put to you the following. He said: "Do you know that there were many villages or small townships, like Janja, where Muslims could live, and many of them remained living there until the end of the war?" And you replied at lines 7 and 8: "Well, no, I wasn't aware of that. I reported on those incidents of ethnic cleansing that occurred while I was in the area." Do you remember that exchange?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like to know what happened in Janja, Mr. Bowen?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd be very interested to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 01292. And this has to be done in private session, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please let me know, Mr. Bowen, when you see the documents on the screen in front of you; the next document, that is. I hope I have the number right. 01292. Do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this is a letter to Dr. Karadzic, dated 5 September 1994, and it reads in the first paragraph: "Already this month, over 1.300 members of the minority communities in the Bijeljina and Janja area have been forced to leave their homes by your authorities and expelled towards Tuzla. Similar departures continue from the Banja Luka region to Croatia, almost 1.000 in the last two weeks. The compulsions from the Bijeljina area are combined with the exaction of significant sums of money (reportedly by a man known as Vojkan) and take place in circumstances that create great hardship for and sometimes threaten the lives of the old and the vulnerable." Now, seeing this document, Mr. Bowen, do you have any comment with regard to Dr. Karadzic's assertion to you as regards the situation for Muslims in Janja?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that document suggests that the situation was very different to the one that he characterised. I'm also interested in the reference to this man Vojkan as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Vojkan during the course of your -- or we discussed a man by the name of Vojkan during the course of your evidence yesterday. Do you see any linkage between or relationship between this document and your evidence in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because Vojkan Djurkovic, Bijeljina, it was about that time that we were filming the -- that documentary. It was in around September of 1994, I'm pretty sure, that we were actually filming, and that was the man who he filmed presiding over that institutionalised process of ethnic cleansing. I wasn't aware -- clearly, it's a private letter. I wasn't aware of this letter at the time, but it does bear out the reporting that we were able to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could have this as the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours. It has to be, because of the provider, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that will be Exhibit P2087, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we're still in private session, and that should probably no longer be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like next to play, in fact, a video-clip which has the 65 ter number 40578. And for my colleagues in the booth, the transcript -- this video-clip will start at the third page of the transcript you were provided with, where the time codes say "00:49:41 to 00:52:30."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will that take more than five minutes from now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me check. I'll forego that and I'll move on to one last item instead, Your Honour, because I might be pushing it a little bit. I'd like to see 65 ter 23081, please. This is an internal document from the Serbian State Security Services, delivered to Frenki Simatovic on 9 April 1994, by an intelligence group sourcing to Mr. Simatovic on events in their area of interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd actually like to take us to page 5 of this six-page document. Now, this last paragraph of this document refers to the situation in Bijeljina also in 1994, a couple of months -- a few months earlier in time than your report from the area. And it refers to the situation there, saying: "In Bijeljina, moving out of the Muslim families, by the exchange of the state commission --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. It's the third page in B/C/S, yes. Continue, Ms. Edgerton, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you: "... by the exchange state commission led Vojislav Djurkovic, aka Puskar or Vojka, still continues, however, the problem is that the said person takes 300 to 500 German marks per head for departure." And the document continues along that vein. And if I could take you about just under halfway through the paragraph, I note the sentence which begins: "However, the entire time, there is information that Puskar is acting under President Karadzic's orders." Further down, it says that information wouldn't be significant if it was not for such a long time in Bijeljina and Janja, and for sure it was also given to the International Red Cross, as well as to the Muslims in Tuzla, Sarajevo and Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see those passages?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any comment with respect to what you've just seen?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I would object to this as being outside the cross-examination. There were no questions about Bijeljina or about this individual. All of that came out in direct examination. I don't think this is proper redirect, and it could lead to more re-cross-examination or an application for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could you help us as to how this was triggered from the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The document -- the passage that I've read specifically refers to the process -- the objectionable process as going on for such a long time in Bijeljina and Janja, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't object earlier this connection with Janja, but there was no evidence provided by the witness about Janja. It was simply the question of Dr. Karadzic to which the witness said he didn't know. So even that was somehow beyond the scope, and I didn't object at the time, but now I think it's objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We tend to agree with the observation of Mr. Robinson; furthermore, that this document is not something that could be appropriately admitted through this witness. And given the time, you will have another opportunity to tender that document later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm done now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Bowen. I appreciate your coming to The Hague to give it. Have a safe journey back home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll need five seconds in private session to reconfirm something confirmed before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We go back to private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume on Monday at 9.00. Have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of January, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
